My son, who is in sixth grade at elementary school, started attending a cram school for the first time about two months ago. He decided to take the entrance examination for a combined junior and senior high school run by the Tokyo metropolitan government.

At the elementary school my son attends, most of the children go to cram school to prepare for entrance examinations.

Against this background, because of my principle that I wanted my son to make every possible effort to study independently, as well as for financial reasons, he had never attended a cram school.

However, my son gradually began to sense the difference in academic ability between himself and the children who attended cram school. He therefore decided to attend one and set his sights on passing the entrance examination for the combined school. Seeing how overwhelmingly happy he seemed to be about attending cram school stirred complicated feelings in me, and I wondered: 'Should I have somehow managed the money to send him earlier, or have I unintentionally stifled the seeds of his development?'

Even so, I still want to tell my son this: I firmly believe that having had plenty of time to think for himself and play during elementary school is a greater source of strength than anything else.

I sincerely hope that, carrying with him the experience of living freely and comfortably during elementary school, he will become someone who can open his own path for himself.

( Note 1: A combined junior and senior high school is an integrated school that combines or connects middle school and high school to provide unified six-year education.

Note 2: Baggage / provisions—here, this refers to spiritual nourishment and things useful for the future.)

The town where I live is called 「Sagamigaoka」. Across the road is a place called Sagamidai.

One day, I was going to register as a foreign resident, so I entered the police box directly opposite to ask for directions to city hall.

「Excuse me, how should I get to city hall?」

A police officer listened to my question and began explaining the route carefully.

「First, take a train bound for Sagamihara from the nearby Odakyu-Sagamihara Station. After getting off at Sagamihara Station, take a bus to city hall. There, that is city hall.」 The police officer took out a map and pointed as he explained.

「Yes, I understand now. Thank you very much for your kind help.」

It took about an hour to get there. I hurriedly wrote my name, nationality, and current address on the application form. But when I handed it to the staff member in charge, he said:

「I'm sorry. You cannot complete that procedure here. The place where you live is not in Sagamihara City. Please go to Zama City.」

「But it clearly has “Sagami” in the name.」

「Sorry to have kept you waiting. Next person, please. Next person, please.」

I felt like saying to myself, 「I'm such an idiot」.

The methods of sorting waste and collection times vary somewhat by area, so be sure to check both carefully.

Burnable waste

Kitchen waste such as fish and vegetables; scrap paper, cigarette butts, sanitary products, clothing, and so on.

How to dispose of it: Put it in a semitransparent plastic bag recommended by the 23 wards, tie the bag tightly so that odors cannot escape, and put it out for collection.

Non-burnable waste

Waste unsuitable for incineration. This includes plastic bags, plastics, metal, glass, leather goods, knives and other cutlery, sewing needles, light bulbs and fluorescent tubes, spray cans, and so on.

How to dispose of it: Put non-dangerous items in a transparent bag through which the contents can be seen, and put it out for collection. Put sewing needles in a bottle or can and close the lid. Wrap light bulbs and broken glass in paper before putting them out.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t8-p1.vietnamese:
Even among Chinese families who became wealthy earlier than others, the tendency of “the husband outside, the wife inside” has begun to become more pronounced. The pattern in which both spouses work to earn money has gradually begun to break down.

As a result, a pattern in which the wife is responsible for the children’s education while the husband concentrates on hunting outside the home (earning money) has gradually begun to take shape. Everyone knows that the amount of time children study and the extent to which their academic ability improves are directly related to their mother’s educational background, but perhaps few people can clearly explain how strong that relationship is.

For this reason, in the spring of this year, the “Japanese-Language Proficiency Test Research Association” conducted a questionnaire survey to investigate the relationship between mothers’ educational backgrounds and the amount of time their children study.

The chart below shows that the higher the mother’s educational background, the lower the percentage of students who answered, “I hardly study at home.” In contrast, it clearly shows that the higher the mother’s educational background, the higher the percentage of students who answered, “About two hours,” “About two and a half hours,” or “Two hours or more.”
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 短期間のパートやアルバイトをして生活する人のことである。
According to the passage, the general modern definition of 「フリーター」 is people who do not work as regular employees but support themselves through short-term part-time jobs.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.explanation: The original sentence is: 「今では、正社員として就職するのではなく、短期間のパート、アルバイトなどをして生活することを言うのが一般的である。」 Its complete meaning is: “Nowadays, this term generally refers to making a living through short-term part-time jobs rather than working as a regular employee.” Grammatically, the passage uses the key N3 structure 「〜のではなく」, which combines with the plain form, such as V-る + のではなく, and means “not A but B,” negating the first option to emphasize the action in the second clause. In addition, 「〜のが一般的である」, formed with the dictionary form V-る + の, expresses a general convention or socially accepted usage. The main trap is choice (b), which borrows a phrase from the beginning of the passage. Pay attention to the contrast between 「最初は…」 (“at first”) and 「今では…」 (“nowadays”) so that you do not choose an outdated definition.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because the passage says that 1980 was when the term 「フリーター」was coined, not that it referred to people born in 1980.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because this refers only to the initial meaning (最初), whereas the current definition (今では) has changed.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is completely consistent with the passage, which states that the common definition today is someone who works short-term part-time jobs to make a living instead of being a regular employee.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t1-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage only states that the number increased sharply after 1990 (1990年以降); it does not say that 1990 was when it reached its peak (ピーク).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) スターが整形手術をしていたこと
The central irony is that the girl wanted to look like her idol and therefore underwent surgery, unaware that the admired star’s own beauty was also the product of cosmetic surgery.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.explanatio: To understand 「①皮肉な話」 (“an ironic story”), look at the sentence immediately before it: 「主人公の少女は、その素敵なスターが実はこっそり整形手術を施していたことをちっとも知らず、自分もあの人そっくりになりたいばかりに、親には内緒で顔を細く見せる手術をしたわけよ」 (“The young protagonist had no idea that the wonderful star had secretly undergone plastic surgery. Because she desperately wanted to look exactly like her, she secretly underwent surgery to make her face look slimmer without telling her parents.”) The key word 「皮肉」 (hiniku) describes an ironic situation in which reality is completely opposite to expectations. It appears with 「V-plain form + ばかりに」, which emphasizes that a single cause led to a rash action with negative consequences. The irony lies in the girl blindly imitating artificial beauty that she believed was natural, pursuing an illusion at any cost. In questions about an underlined expression, always focus on the context immediately before it to identify the correct referent. Do not be distracted by later tragic developments, such as high medical bills or selling blood in choice (c).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) The irony is that the girl idolized the star and underwent surgery to imitate the star’s face without knowing that the star had secretly undergone cosmetic surgery as well.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage contains no information saying that the star does not have a slender face.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The fact that the surgery costs more than expected is merely a circumstance leading to the decision to sell blood for money; it is not the irony referred to in the underlined part.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) This is incorrect because the passage clearly states that after the surgery, the girl became noticeably prettier (めっきりきれいになった), which is the opposite of this statement.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 新しい形の見合いをする。
Young people without time to date turned to matchmaking agencies, and the passage describes using these services as a new form of arranged matchmaking.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.explanatio: The direct evidence is the sentence: 「日本には昔から見合い結婚があるが、こんな会社を使うのは新しい見合いのしかたと言えるかもしれない。」 (“Japan has had arranged marriage since long ago, but using companies like these might be considered a new form of arranged matchmaking.”) The key grammar pattern is 「〜と言える / と言えるかもしれない」, which combines with the plain form and expresses an objective evaluation or a new perspective on something (“it can be said that...” or “it might be considered...” ). Thus, the author regards busy young people’s use of companies to introduce dating partners as a modern form of arranged matchmaking. To answer this type of question, beware of the keyword trap in choice (b): although the service name remains unchanged, the question deliberately switches the action from “using the service” (使う) to “working” (働く).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage only mentions traditional arranged marriage (見合い結婚) as a custom from the past, not as a solution used by busy young people today.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) This option is misleading because the busy young people use the matchmaking company's services (使う); they do not go there to work (働く).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This choice is completely correct because the author states that having a company introduce people for dating can be considered a new form of matchmaking (新しい見合いのしかた).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage does not mention young people giving up and abandoning both matchmaking and marriage.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 近所付き合いの大切さに気づいた。
Taking part fully in the festival helped the author realize the importance of mutual support within the community during disasters. This changed the author's previous indifference and revealed the value of relationships with neighbors.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.explanatio: The strongest evidence is found in the concluding sentence: 「今回の盆踊り大会への参加をきっかけに、今後は近所の人たちとも、これまで以上に話をして、顔も覚えていこうと思いました。」 (“After taking part in this Bon Odori festival, I decided that from now on I would talk with my neighbors more than before and try to remember their faces.”) The key grammar pattern 「N + をきっかけに」 combines with a noun referring to an event and expresses a turning point or opportunity that brings about a major change in awareness or behavior. It is used together with the required form 「V-ない (remove ない) + なくては」 (“must do”) in the preceding sentence to emphasize community awareness. The author had previously shown little interest in the neighborhood (「関心が薄かった」), but helping prepare for the festival firsthand enabled a deeper understanding of the nature and importance of neighborhood relationships (「近所付き合いの大切さ」), especially during emergencies such as natural disasters. Do not confuse incidental details with the central lesson: the children playing in choice (b) merely prompted the author’s thinking, whereas a question asking what the author “gained” (得たもの) requires attention to the character’s change in awareness and future behavior at the end of the passage.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage does not mention the author feeling joy or excitement from the festival; instead, it emphasizes a change in awareness of the community.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The detail about children running and playing carefree is merely an observed image that evokes emotion; “encountering smiles” is not something the author took in.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) By participating in the festival, the author realized the importance of helping one another during disasters and decided to interact proactively and remember the faces of the neighbors.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage only mentions that many people in the new residential area did not know one another; it does not say that the author recognized that the population was large.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 兄とけんかをしたばかりだから
The eldest daughter initially ignored her brother’s call because the siblings often argued, and they had just had a fight that very day.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.explanatio: To find the reason for the younger sister’s ignoring behavior in underlined sentence ①, look directly at the sentence immediately before it: 「いつも口げんかが絶えない二人。その日も言い争いをしたばかり。」 (The two children are always arguing, and that day they had just finished quarrelling again.) The key N3 grammar pattern「V-た + ばかり」expresses an action or event that has just been completed recently, according to the speaker’s subjective perception. The noun「言い争い」is also synonymous with「けんか」(quarrelling, conflict). Because the siblings had just had an argument, the younger sister was still sulking, naturally causing her to ignore her older brother’s urging. In reading-comprehension questions asking about cause and effect, stay close to the adjacent sentence that explains the characters’ psychology, rather than being distracted by details that merely describe the surrounding situation, such as not having gone to bed or being in the room.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) Correct: the passage clearly states that the two brothers are always arguing and had just argued that day as well (その日も言い争いをしたばかり), which directly caused the younger brother to ignore him at first.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The fact that the younger sibling was still awake (まだ起きていた) was simply the actual state at that moment; it does not explain why the girl ignored her older brother.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage only says that the younger sibling was staying shut in her room (部屋にこもっていた); it gives no information that she was doing something she liked.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The fact that it was already late at night (夜やや遅く) is merely the setting when the older brother returned from school, not the reason the younger sibling ignored him.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 方向音痴のせいである。
The author admits that frequently losing their way is not necessarily due to age, but rather to inherently being directionally challenged (方向音痴).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.explanatio: The key evidence for answering the question is the sentence:「考えてみると、これは年のせいというより、もともと方向音痴なのかもしれない。」(“When I think about it, rather than being caused by age, perhaps I have always been bad with directions.”). The author uses the important N3 grammar pattern「～というより」with a plain form or noun. It means “rather than saying A, B is more accurate” and is used when the speaker gently rejects a common assumption and presents a more accurate explanation. Combined with the adverb「もともと」(originally, by nature) and the speculation pattern「～のかもしれない」(perhaps), it indicates that the fundamental cause of the author’s losing their way is an inherent lack of direction sense (方向音痴). Learners may easily be trapped into choosing (b),「年のせいである」(it is caused by age), because the beginning of the passage mentions declining memory. However, in the pattern「A というより B」, the author’s actual view is always in clause B, while clause A is being rejected.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The police officer enthusiastically helped the author find the way; the officer was not the reason the author became lost.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Although the passage initially mentions declining memory, the author denies that age is the cause through the expression「年のせいというより」.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) The author directly identifies the root cause of being directionally confused: they are naturally directionally challenged (方向音痴).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The roughly drawn map is merely the object the author blames for not being able to find the way; it is not the cause of getting lost.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 運動のできる場所が減っているから
The author identifies the direct reason children play sports outdoors less often: spaces where they can exercise are shrinking, with parks banning ball games, overgrown grass, and concrete roads that make children afraid of falling.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.explanatio: The direct basis for the answer is the second sentence of the passage: 「僕はその理由に運動できる場所が減ったことが挙げられると思います。」. It means: "I think one reason that can be cited is that the number of places where people can exercise has decreased." The key structure 「N に + [plain form + こと] + が挙げられる」uses a formal, objective passive/potential form of the transitive verb 挙げる. It is commonly used in explanatory or argumentative writing to present a representative cause or example related to N. For this question, learners may mistakenly choose (b) because parks are mentioned repeatedly. However, the key reading skill is to clearly distinguish between "the conditions for using the space" (parks have signs prohibiting ball games or grass that has grown too long) and "the number of spaces" (the passage gives no information that the number of parks has decreased).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) Incorrect because the passage does not mention electronic games or indoor games becoming popular at all.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because the author only complains about warning signs and excessively long grass in the park; they never say that the number of parks has decreased.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is correct because the author clearly states that the places where people can exercise have decreased (“運動できる場所が減った”), and then lists various difficulties at specific locations.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The author says only that they were afraid of falling on the concrete surface and therefore could not play wholeheartedly; it does not say that the wide road had become dangerous.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 自分の道を自分の力で開いてほしい。
In the final sentence of the passage, the mother states that her central wish is for her son to create his own future through his own efforts.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.explanatio: The key evidence lies in the final sentence of the passage: 「伸びやかに過ごした小学校時代を糧に、自分の道を自分で切り開く人になって欲しいと強く願っている。」 (roughly: “I sincerely hope that my child will use those carefree elementary school years as a foundation and become someone who can carve out their own path.”) Grammatically, 「V-て + ほしい」 combines with the particle に to indicate the person whose action is desired, expressing the speaker’s strong wish or hope that someone else will do something. The phrase 「切り開く」 (to carve out or open up a path oneself) is semantically equivalent to 「開く」 in the answer choice. The central point is that although the mother has some passing concerns about finances or academic ability, deep down she firmly believes in the independence her child developed through years of free thinking during childhood. In N3 reading-comprehension questions about an author’s feelings or wishes, learners can easily be misled by distractors such as (a) and (c) because the passage mentions examinations and extra lessons. The key is to focus on sentences containing words that directly express emotions or wishes, such as 「伝えたい」, 「〜てほしい」, and 「願っている」, which often appear near the end of the passage and reveal the author’s main intention.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage does not mention a mother wanting her child to study competitively so as not to fall behind their peers.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) This choice accurately expresses the mother’s wish in the final sentence: that her child use childhood experiences as preparation for opening a path of their own.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The decision to take the entrance examination for an integrated school arose from the child’s own wish after noticing the difference in academic ability. The mother did not pressure the child to pass.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t17-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The mother was only blaming herself because of the family's financial circumstances; the passage contains no detail showing that she wanted her child not to worry about the family.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) もったいない
The author grew up during a time of material scarcity and therefore felt 「もったいない」 (“what a waste”), hesitating to throw things away and instead putting them in a drawer.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.explanatio: The key sentence is: 「だが、モノの乏しい時代に育った者には①抵抗感があり、捨てようとしたものを再度しまい込むことが多い。」 (“However, people who grew up in a time when material goods were scarce often feel reluctant and put away again things they had tried to throw out.”) Here, the noun 「抵抗感」 (“a feeling of resistance or reluctance”) combines with 「が」 in 「抵抗感がある」 to describe psychological hesitation about throwing things away. This corresponds exactly to 「もったいない」, an い-adjective expressing regret over wasting something that still has value. The volitional form 「捨てようとする」 followed by putting the item back away 「再度しまい込む」 highlights that the reluctance comes from memories of hardship. To avoid the trap, note that choice (a), 「おしくない」, comes from 「惜しい」 (“regrettable”), which is close in meaning to 「もったいない」, but the negative ending 「～くない」 changes it to mean “not regrettable,” the complete opposite.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because 「おしくない」 means “not regrettable” or “not worth regretting,” which is the complete opposite of the author's reluctance to throw things away and decision to store them.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because 「あきない」means “not get bored”; it does not express hesitation or reluctance to throw something away while cleaning up.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) 「もったいない」expresses regret over waste and the feeling that something should not be thrown away, accurately explaining the hesitation of someone who lived through a period of scarcity.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「あぶない」means “dangerous,” which is completely unsuitable for the context of tidying a household drawer.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 太鼓を叩くこと
The two girls went from never having held drumsticks to practicing and being able to play the drums themselves at the festival.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.explanatio: The basis is the sentence from paragraph 2: 「太鼓のバチなど握ったこともなかった娘たちが、今では叩けるようになるまで上達した。」 (“The girls, who had never even held drumsticks before, have now improved enough to be able to play the drums.”) The key grammar is 「V potential form + ようになる」. The potential-form verb 「叩ける」 (“can play or hit”) with 「ようになる」 describes a change in ability from being unable to do something to becoming able to do it after learning and practice. Test takers may choose (a) or (b) if they only notice the actions 「花車やみこしを担ぐ」 (“carry festival floats or portable shrines”), but these are general festival activities performed by everyone in the town, not skills acquired by the two girls. Choice (d), 「手を叩く」 (“clap one’s hands”), is a vocabulary trap using the same verb 「叩く」 and does not fit the context of playing festival drums, 「太鼓を叩く」.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) Carrying a flower float (花車を担ぐこと) is a communal town procession activity, not something the two girls learned.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) Similarly, carrying a portable shrine (みこしを担ぐこと) is a community festival custom, and the author never mentions that the two children can carry one.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) The passage states that after practicing for some time, the two girls improved remarkably and became able to play the drums (叩けるようになる).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Clapping one’s hands (手を叩くこと) is not mentioned anywhere in the passage; it is merely a distractor based on the verb 叩く.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t2-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 投資 し た 金 が 無駄 に な る 。
The government and local authorities invested 76.1 billion yen in employment-support measures, but 98.8% of people in the NEET group did not use the support facilities at all. As a result, the investment was largely ineffective and became wasted money.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t2-q1.explanation: The basis is the sentence from the passage: 「しかし、ニート層の98.8% がニート支援施設を全く利用したことがないというアンケート結果もあるとおり、761億円を投資した若者の雇用対策はあまり ② 効果が現れていない。」 (However, as the survey results show, 98.8% of people in the NEET group have never used a NEET support facility at all, so the youth employment measures funded with an investment of 76.1 billion yen have hardly produced any results.) The grammar pattern 「〜とおり」 (just as/as) combines with 「全く〜ない」 (not at all) and 「あまり〜ない」 (not very much) to show that although the government spent a very large amount of money (761億円を投資した), it produced little practical benefit because the intended users did not use the facilities. In other words, the invested money was wasted or became useless (投資した金が無駄になる).

In the context of a fierce battle, the raised 「白い旗」 is crucial because it shows that they are not carrying weapons intended to cause harm, helping the other side approach without fear. This identifies the known topic in the first clause and focuses attention on the key information in the second. default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t32-q1.explanatio: Grammatically, the So-series demonstrative 「そういうふうに」 (“in that way”) refers back to content mentioned earlier in the context. Combined with 「〜べきではない」 (V-る + べきではない: should not do something according to morality or common sense), the complete meaning is: “However, we should not think about greetings in that way.” The direct evidence appears in the first paragraph, immediately before the contrastive conjunction 「だが」. The author states: 「『おはよう』とか、『こんにちは』とかいうあいさつの言葉は考えてみれば、意味のない言葉のようにも思われます」 and 「まったく意味がない言葉だという意見もあるようです」 (“If you think about it, greetings such as ‘ohayou’ and ‘konnichiwa’ may seem like meaningless words... Some people also seem to think that they are completely meaningless.”). Thus, the “way of thinking” the author rejects is the idea that greetings have no meaning (あいさつに意味はない). To solve this type of question, learners should look for information immediately before a contrastive connector such as 「だが」 to identify what is being rejected, rather than confusing it with (a), the claim made afterward. They should also watch out for distractor (c), which uses the keyword 「理解しにくい」 (“difficult to understand”); in the passage, this is merely supporting evidence used to explain the idea of meaninglessness, not the main argument.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t32-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because it asserts the importance of greetings, as explained in the later paragraphs, contradicting the negative view that the author is trying to refute.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t32-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct because the underlined phrase replaces the statement in paragraph 1 that greetings are meaningless words (「意味のない言葉」「まったく意味がない言葉」).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t32-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because「理解しにくい」in the passage is merely an example explaining why saying good morning near noon is meaningless, not a general statement about greetings.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t33-q1.explanatio: The direct evidence is the quotation: 「和室(日本古来の畳の部屋)に入る時は、必ず履物を脱ぐ。」, meaning: “When entering a Japanese-style room—a traditional Japanese room with tatami mats—you must always remove your footwear.” Grammatically, the dictionary-form structure「V-る + 時（は）」combines with the adverb「必ず」(always, without fail) to emphasize a fixed rule or social convention. In terms of vocabulary,「履物」is a general term covering both outdoor shoes (外靴) and indoor slippers (スリッパ/室内履き). Therefore, removing one’s「履物」means entering in bare feet (「素足」) or wearing socks. Do not confuse removing outdoor shoes at the 玄関 with removing all footwear before entering a 和室; slippers must not be worn on tatami.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.verdict:

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.explanatio: The opening definition provides the key evidence: 「地球の温暖化とは二酸化炭素などの温室効果ガスの増加により、地球の気温が高まり、自然や生活環境に各種の悪影響が生じる現象です。」 (“Global warming is the phenomenon in which the Earth’s temperature rises due to an increase in greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, causing various harmful effects on the natural environment and living conditions.”) The key cause-expression grammar is 「noun + により」, which has a formal tone and is common in objective argumentative or written language. It states the reason leading to the change or result in the following clause. Learners may be trapped by answer choice (b) because the passage repeatedly mentions CO₂. However, the production (発生) of CO₂ is a normal natural process during respiration; it becomes harmful only when greenhouse gases increase excessively, beyond what is necessary (増加 / 必要以上に大量). Also, when solving cause-and-effect reading questions, clearly distinguish the cause from the result: answer choice (a), “the temperature rises,” is actually the result of heat being trapped near the Earth’s surface, not the original cause.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is a result or manifestation of global warming, not a cause of it.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The production of CO₂ is a natural process through respiration; it becomes a cause only when the amount of this gas increases excessively.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is correct according to the definition at the beginning of the passage: global warming occurs because of an increase in greenhouse gases.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t34-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage does not mention any increase or population explosion.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t35-q1.explanatio: The relevant sentence is: 「そのほかに、左右二つの目の働きによって、物が遠くにあるか、近くにあるかを見分けることができるのです。」 (“In addition, the function of the two eyes allows us to distinguish whether an object is far away or nearby.”) This sentence uses 「Noun + によって」 to express means or cause (“through” or “thanks to”), together with the paired question structure 「plain form + か、～か」 (“whether... or...”), used to distinguish between two contrasting possibilities. The author emphasizes that the ability to perceive depth and locate objects as near or far depends directly on the functioning of both eyes. Therefore, by inverse reasoning, when observing with only one eye (片方の目だけ), this ability is impaired and distance becomes unclear (はっきりしない). To avoid trap choice (d), note that a wide field of view (広い範囲) results from the eyes being separated (離れていて). Losing vision in one eye can only narrow the field of view, not widen it.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t35-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because recognizing shapes is a basic visual function of the eyes in general, not a consequence of seeing with only one eye.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t35-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The color of an object can normally be recognized through sight. The passage does not say that seeing with one eye makes colors difficult to distinguish.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t35-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) This is correct because the passage states that two eyes help distinguish whether an object is far away or nearby; therefore, using only one eye makes it impossible to determine distance accurately.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t35-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) A wide field of vision is possible because of the distance between the two eyes. Looking with only one eye narrows the field of view.

The reason international exchange is widely discussed is that it is essential for countries to understand one another and thereby live together harmoniously in peace.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t36-q1.explanatio: To identify the author’s reason, focus on the sentence stating the purpose: 「たしかに、世界中の国々が仲良く平和に生活していくためには、言葉や文化の違いがあっても理解し合って、話し合いをしなければなりません。」 (“Indeed, for countries around the world to live together peacefully and harmoniously, people must understand and talk with one another despite differences in language and culture.”) The key grammar is 「V-る／Nの ＋ ため（に）」, which combines with a dictionary-form verb to express a volitional purpose (“in order to...”), together with 「～ていく」, which conveys maintaining a positive state from the present into the future. Thus, striving to understand and communicate is the means of achieving the ultimate goal of building a peaceful world. Avoid the trap in choice (a): although the passage contains 「異なる」, it says 「国や文化や言葉の異なる人たち」, not 「民族」 (“ethnic groups”), and understanding is the means, not the ultimate purpose.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t36-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage discusses differences in countries, languages, and cultures, but never mentions the purpose of understanding different peoples (民族).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t36-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage contains no information stating that international exchange is lacking or insufficient (足りない).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t36-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) The author clearly states that overcoming barriers to communication is intended to help countries live together harmoniously and peacefully.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t36-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The article focuses on living together peacefully and does not mention developing world culture (世界文化を発展させる).

It appears with the N3 pattern 「N1から始まってN2まで」 (“starting with N1 and extending to N2”), which lists examples from a representative starting point to a broader range and emphasizes the variety of heat-based cooking techniques. The direct evidence is: 「魚というので、すぐ思い浮かべるのはサシミですね。生はどうにも口に合わないとおっしゃるかたがたには①加熱料理をお勧めします。」 This means: “When we think of fish, sashimi is what immediately comes to mind. This makes it easy to eliminate the other choices, because タマゴ, 天ぷら, and マンジュウ are all examples in the passage of dishes prepared with heat, such as boiling (ゆでる), frying (揚げる), and steaming (むす).

It presents an objective, factual reason for the result 「まだ決めていません」. The phrase 「一人では」 in the correct choice clarifies the situation: she likes the apartment, but the cost is too much for one person, so she needs a 「ルームメート」 to share the expense. For N3 reading questions of this type, follow the contrastive connector 「でも」 (“but”) to identify the central problem. Do not be distracted by details such as the landlord seeming kind 「優しそう」 (choice a) or the narrator thinking of his older brother’s friend (choice b).

The idiom 「夢のまた夢」 refers to something completely remote, imaginary, and impossible to realize in everyday life. In the context of the reading, company employees are so busy with work that spending time enjoying personal hobbies is impossible.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-q2.explanatio: The evidence appears in paragraph 3: 「こうなると、趣味を楽しむなど、②夢のまた夢で、アパートと会社の往復で1年が終わってしまう。」 This means: “When things reach this point, doing things such as enjoying one’s hobbies is a dream far beyond reach, and the year ends with nothing but commuting back and forth between the apartment and the company.” 「夢のまた夢」 is an idiomatic noun phrase, often used with 「だ」 or 「で」, emphasizing a fanciful or entirely unattainable wish. The author uses it to portray the extreme busyness of Japanese office workers: if even basic activities such as dating and exercising are difficult, pursuing personal hobbies is even more impossible. Do not interpret it literally as in option (a), “dream after dream,” or confuse it with the positive expression 「夢のような」 (“wonderful, dreamlike”) in (c). 「夢のまた夢」 always strongly implies that something is virtually impossible.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-q2.explanatio: To understand the essence of「情緒」(a soul capable of being moved by beauty), the key evidence is the sentence:「あまりに美しい月を帰り道で見た長男は、それを誰かに伝えたいようで、長女を誘ったのであった」(That night was the autumn full moon night. On his way home, the eldest son saw an astonishingly beautiful moon and, wanting to share it with someone, invited his sister.) The author emphasizes this emotion through the important N3 pattern「N + ならではの + N」, which follows a noun directly and praises a positive quality unique to that particular subject, in「自然に湧き上がるこの気持ちは人ならではのものだろう」. This states that the ability to be moved by nature’s beauty and want to share it is a quality unique to human beings. The complete translation of the underlined passage「長男がその夜、いつもけんかし合う長女と並んで満月を眺めた様子を想像するとあったかい気持ちになり、情緒はちゃんと育っているなと安心したのであった」is: “When I imagined the eldest son standing beside his younger sister, whom he was always arguing with, and looking at the full moon that night, I felt warm inside and was reassured that his emotional sensitivity was developing in a healthy way.” Students may be tempted by (a) because the older brother invited his sister outside. However, the key is to distinguish the cause that aroused the emotion—the beautiful moon—from the action taken to share it—inviting a family member to look at it together. Here,「情緒」refers specifically to aesthetic sensitivity, not merely affection for one’s sister.

A useful strategy is to identify the action keyword in the question (「誘った」) and then look immediately before it for the corresponding reason (「それを誰かに伝えたいようで」). It is accompanied by the adverb「とにかく」, meaning “first of all” or “in any case,” used in an urgent situation to prioritize calming down before dealing with the problem. For questions asking why (どうして), look for the direct connection in the neighboring sentence and identify paraphrases. Here,「目指す建物が見つからない」is generalized as「探しているものが見つからない」in answer choice (d). The key expression uses 「V-dictionary form + より」 to mean "rather than doing V, it is better to do what follows," combined with the imperative 「聞け」, which gives the phrase the force of a maxim: ask someone for directions as soon as you become lost. Test takers may easily choose option (d) because the character wandered around trying to find the way earlier in the passage. The monkey’s careful peeling of each layer of the shallot skin (一枚また一枚) provides direct evidence for this general observation. In reading-comprehension questions asking what was learned from an observation (分かったこと), prioritize the general topic sentence at the beginning rather than being distracted by minor details, such as the struggle in option (a) or the reminder to visitors at the end of the passage (option (d)).

It conveys an earnest, urgent request that someone pay close attention or avoid an action for safety or to prevent bad consequences. The author’s impression is identified by the final sentence: 「見物の皆さんにくれぐれもお願いします。猿が食べないものを与えないでください。」 (“I earnestly ask all visitors: please do not give the monkeys things they do not eat”). A baby monkey mistook a scallion for fruit and carefully peeled away its layers, but because it consisted only of layered leaves, it never found the inside (「なかなか実が出てこない」). The monkey became disappointed, and another monkey stole it, causing a noisy scramble. The author therefore felt sorry for the monkeys (かわいそう) being treated as entertainment. default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t42-q4.explanatio: Based on the note found in the document:「ありがとうございました。助かりました。④あきらめていました。」, the key to this question is understanding the true meaning of the verb「あきらめる」(to give up, abandon hope). The pattern「あきらめていました」combines the progressive form「〜ていた」with the Group 2 verb「あきらめる」and describes a prolonged psychological state that began when the item was lost: the person had completely given up and no longer hoped for something they believed could not be recovered. The complete meaning is: “Thank you very much. You really saved me. I had already given up hope of finding my key.” Thus, the owner wrote this because they were convinced that once the key had been dropped, it would never return (落としたカギはもう戻らないだろう). Many test takers mistakenly choose (d) because the author returned the key quickly, after only two days. However, the key distinction is that「あきらめる」comes from believing that the lost item was gone for good; it does not concern whether the owner expected to get it back quickly or slowly.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t42-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) This choice is incorrect because “giving up hope” (あきらめる) is completely opposite to having continued to wait for the key to return (ずっと待っていた).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t42-q4.why.1: ✓ (b) This is correct because the person who dropped the key wrote「aきらめていました」based on the thought that once the key was lost, there was no possibility of getting it back.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t42-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) This choice is incorrect because the person gave up immediately after losing it, not because waiting too long caused them to run out of patience (もう待てなかった).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t42-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) This choice is incorrect because the key point of “giving up” is believing that something has been lost forever, not being surprised at getting the key back shortly afterward.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 北海道は環境もいいし、地元のものも食べられるから
Hokkaido has a wonderful, clean natural environment and abundant fresh local food, which makes the author love the place and not want to leave.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.explanatio: From a grammar perspective, underlined sentence ② contains 「～かもしれない」, which follows the plain form (普通形) to express a tentative possibility. It is combined with the negative form 「V-たくなくなる」(gradually lose the desire to do something). The complete translation is: "By then, I may not want to return to Tokyo anymore." The reasons for this feeling are clearly expressed through the scenery and food, as shown in the original quotations: 「北海道は東京と違って、空気もおいしいし、景色もすばらしいところである」and「北海道はすばらしい景色だけでなく、おいしい食べ物も有名である」. Choice (a) uses the parallel reason-listing pattern 「～し、～し」(plain form + し), summarizing both the beautiful living environment and the local produce and fresh fish that cause the author to eat too much. In N3 reading comprehension, focus on the overall meaning of the passage and avoid choices that overstate narrow details, such as (b) and (c), or distort the original information, such as (d).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) This choice accurately encompasses the two reasons the author loves Hokkaido: its clean natural environment and its fresh local food.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage only says that the author drank fresh milk there for the first time; it does not claim that this drink is available only in Hokkaido.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) Comparing vegetables from Hokkaido with those from Tokyo is merely an illustrative example of fresh, delicious food, not the general reason the author does not want to return.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) This choice directly contradicts the passage because the author states at the beginning that they do not dislike Tokyo (「東京は嫌いではないが」).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 東京では味わえない本物のミルクが飲める。
In Hokkaido, the author tastes rich, fresh milk for the first time—milk with a flavor like fresh cream that cannot be experienced in Tokyo, where the milk tastes as thin as water.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.explanatio: Choice (d) means: "You can drink genuine fresh milk that cannot be enjoyed in Tokyo." It uses the negative potential form 「味わえない」, the potential form of the Group 1 transitive verb 味わう: 味わえる, then 味わえない. This expresses an objective circumstance that prevents the action. The statement is fully supported by the narrator’s words: 「今朝起きて生まれて初めて生ミルクを飲んだ。生ミルクは生クリームのように特別なおいしさがある。今思うと、東京で飲んでいたミルクは水のようである。」 Through the comparison pattern 「～のように」(like...), the author contrasts the bland, water-like milk in Tokyo with the rich, creamy fresh milk in Hokkaido, emphasizing that only this place offers the genuine product. Test takers may be tempted by choice (b) because of the keyword 「花のじゅうたん」(carpet of flowers), but that scenery belongs to the place called Furano (富良野という所); the passage does not mention any park (公園).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage clearly states that Hokkaido has many kinds of fish, from the sea, rivers, and lakes (種類がたくさんある), which is the opposite of the claim that there are not many varieties.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) The author describes an expansive field of purple flowers in Furano, like a floral carpet; the passage does not mention a large park.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) The author only praises the vegetables for being fresh because they are grown directly on farms, and does not mention high nutritional value or expensive prices.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t43-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) The author describes drinking exceptionally delicious fresh milk for the first time in Hokkaido, whereas the milk sold in Tokyo was watery and lacked this authentic flavor.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) せっかく盗んできた切符が売れなくなること
The thief regrets that the tickets worth 50 million yen, which he went to great trouble to steal, have become worthless and impossible to resell because the city decided to stop charging tolls on all bridges starting this morning.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q2.explanatio: The direct evidence comes from an office worker's comment: 「今度、いちばん残念がっている人は泥棒だろう。」 (This time, the person who is probably most disappointed is the thief), immediately after the information 「市役所は一晩会議をして最後に全市の橋を渡る料金徴収は今朝0時からやめることにしたそうである。」 (The city hall reportedly held an all-night meeting and finally decided to stop collecting tolls on all the city's bridges from midnight this morning.) Once crossing the bridges became completely free (通行無料), the stolen tickets worth 50 million yen had no remaining practical value, meaning that the thief could no longer sell them for money. Grammatically, the key adverb せっかく, often used with the past form V-た, conveys the sense of having gone to the trouble of doing something, making choice (a) fully express the regret that the effort ultimately became worthless because circumstances changed unexpectedly. The key distinction is to focus on the psychological keyword 「残念」, meaning disappointment or regret when a plan fails, in connection with the tickets' value, rather than making assumptions based on real-world logic, such as the thief fearing a police investigation (b) or worrying about being arrested (c).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) This choice is correct because the city decided to abolish bridge tolls at midnight this morning, making the tickets the thief had just stolen worthless for use or resale.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) This is incorrect because the passage only says that the police are investigating and that the clues remain unclear; this is not what the thief regrets most.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 今度の事件で橋利用料金を払わなくてもよくなってとても喜んでいる気持ち
The central reason is that the city decided to stop charging bridge tolls after the ticket theft, freeing the author from the costly burden paid over the previous three years and bringing great joy.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.explanatio: The pattern 「〜おかげで / おかげさまで」 follows a noun with の or a verb or adjective in plain form (普通形). It expresses deep gratitude for a good result brought about by someone or something. Here, 「泥棒さん、おかげさまで」 has a humorous tone and can be translated as: “Mr. Thief, thanks to you” or “Thanks to you, Mr. Thief.” The author had complained about paying a great deal of money for years: 「私は車を買ってからもう三年間で、20万も払ってしまった」. Because of the theft, however, the authorities decided to stop collecting bridge tolls: 「全市の橋を渡る料金徴収は今朝0時からやめることにした」. This leads to the final reaction: 「心の中で『泥棒さん、おかげさまで』と喜んだ」. The author feels delighted because an unexpected event has indirectly relieved the burden of regular toll payments. To avoid the trap in (a), which refers to no longer having to wait in a long line 「長い列を作って待っていた」, identify the character’s greatest concern: the financial burden 「料金はたいへんだった」. Being able to cross the bridge for free is therefore the direct and essential reason for this humorous gratitude.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) Not having to wait in line was merely an observable situation that morning, not the underlying reason the author was delighted and thanked the thief.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) This is incorrect because the author’s emotion at that moment was joy (喜んだ) at an outcome favorable to them, not surprise at receiving the news early.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because the passage does not mention the author looking forward to buying tickets; the actual feeling is happiness, not relief.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) The ticket theft caused the city to stop collecting the bridge toll, so the author no longer had to pay the expensive daily fee and felt extremely happy.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 世の中、何が良いことで何が悪いことか分からない。
Stealing bridge tickets was an unfortunate and wrong act, but it ultimately led the city to make bridge crossings free, bringing great benefits and happiness to residents.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.explanatio: The passage ends with the key detail: 「今度、いちばん残念がっている人は泥棒だろう。」ここまで聞いて、私は首を縦に振って、心の中で「泥棒さん、おかげさまで」と喜んだ。 The complete translation is: "Hearing this, I nodded in agreement and rejoiced inwardly, saying, 'Dear thief, I have you to thank for this!'" The key N3 grammar pattern is 「〜おかげで／おかげさまで」, used with the plain form of a verb or adjective, or noun + の. It expresses gratitude by identifying the cause of a positive result, creating humorous contrast because a bad act of theft unexpectedly brought practical benefits to the residents. A common trap is choice (c), since both involve opposing concepts of good and bad. Pay attention to the sequence of events and the cause-and-effect relationship: (c) states that "something bad will happen after something good," whereas in the story, something negative happens first and then leads to a beneficial result. Thus, the entire story humorously illustrates the idea that fortune and misfortune are unpredictable and that one should not hastily judge an event as lucky or unlucky, which corresponds exactly to choice (d).
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage focuses on the irony of a bad event leading to a beneficial outcome for local residents; it does not discuss the rapid pace of social change.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) The toll station unexpectedly abolishing the bridge toll overnight shows that life is always subject to unforeseen changes rather than remaining unchanging.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because in the passage, the bad event—the theft—happens first and then produces a positive outcome for the people using the road, which is completely opposite to the sequence described in this choice.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t46-q4.why.3: ✓ (d) Correct, because the theft, which seemed like a disaster, unexpectedly became an opportunity for local residents to cross the bridge free of charge, reflecting the idea that life is unpredictable and we cannot know what will turn out to be good or bad.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 人間関係がよくない。
The main reason is that relationships among the company’s employees are tense: the coworkers only flatter their superior and lazily doze off, while the current manager constantly nitpicks, leaving him extremely dissatisfied.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q2.explanatio: The author expresses frustration with the work environment: 「その上、一緒に働いている人たちもあまり魅力がないんです。同僚の山田さんはいつも上司にごまをすることを考えている人で、上司がいないときは居眠りばかりしているんです。そして、今の上司は私の仕事にけちをつけるのが好きで、頭に来ることがあります。」 ("Moreover, the people I work with are not very appealing either. My colleague Yamada is always thinking about flattering the boss and does nothing but doze off when the boss is away. My current boss likes to find fault with my work, which sometimes makes me angry.") The idiom 「けちをつける」, used in 「[noun/action] にけちをつける」, has a negative tone and means to nitpick or criticize someone’s faults in a petty manner. The pattern 「Vて + ばかりいる」 describes a bad action that is repeated constantly, expressing the speaker’s annoyance or disapproval. The combination of a flattering, lazy colleague and a critical, fault-finding supervisor shows that Kimura’s main source of irritation is the poor internal workplace relationships (人間関係). Choice (b) is only background information (「小さな会社」), not the author’s complaint. Choice (a) is ruled out by the contrastive conjunction 「しかし」 followed by the statement that the salary is not bad (「給料は悪くありません」).

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) The author does not mention anywhere in the letter whether commuting to work is convenient or inconvenient.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) しばらく今の会社にいてそれから出ようと思っている。
Kimura plans to continue working at his current company for another six months to save money for tuition before leaving to study in the United States.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q3.explanatio: The key sentence in paragraph 3 is: 「もちろん、この会社で長く働くつもりはありませんが、もう半年ここで働いて、将来アメリカのビジネススクールで勉強するための学費を貯めようと思っています。」 Its complete translation is: “Of course, I do not intend to work at this company for a long time, but I plan to work here for another six months to save tuition for studying at a business school in the United States in the future.” The pattern 「V-ようと思っている」 expresses a plan that the speaker considered previously and continues to maintain. The sequence of actions is linked with the te-form 「V-て」 (働いて), showing that the speaker will first save enough tuition and then study abroad. This corresponds to the paraphrase replacing 「もう半年」 with 「しばらく」 in the correct choice. Be careful with the distractor 「すぐ」 (“immediately”) in (a) and (b), which directly contradicts the six-month timeframe. Choice (d) is also an incorrect inference: the author only asks the teacher to write a recommendation letter before July and does not intend to leave urgently.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) This choice is incorrect because he cannot go to the United States immediately; he still has to work to save tuition and submit his application before summer.

The writer is contacting Teacher Tanaka to announce plans to study at a business school in the United States and earnestly ask him to write a recommendation letter.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t48-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 人の事は自分に関係がないと思っているから
The pedestrians did not stop to look at the woman in trouble on the cold night because they were indifferent and considered other people’s problems unrelated to themselves.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t48-q2.explanatio: The direct evidence is in the penultimate sentence of Passage 4: 「しかし、私の後ろを通る人たちは、その女の人を見ないで、寒い夜道を急いで歩いているだけだった。」 (However, the people passing behind me did not look at the woman; they merely hurried along the cold nighttime road.) The key grammar is 「V-ないで」 (doing V2 without doing V1) together with 「～ているだけ」 (indicating limitation, “merely doing ...”). This clearly conveys the cold indifference of the passersby as they deliberately ignored the person in trouble. They simply kept walking because they regarded what happened in the street as someone else’s business (人の事), completely unrelated to themselves (自分に関係がない). The main potential confusion is answer choice (d), which contains the keywords 「警官」 and 「怖い」. However, the reading strategy is to identify the subject correctly: 「少し怖くなった」 describes the author’s own feeling (“I”), not the passersby’s.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t48-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) This is correct because hurriedly walking past without looking shows indifference, as though the other person's misfortune has nothing to do with them.

default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t48-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) ニューヨークで二つの体験をした。
The letter was written to share the writer’s first two experiences after arriving in New York: enjoying Christmas shopping and witnessing an unsettling incident on the street.
default.q.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t48-q3.explanatio: In his letter to Blanc, Koizumi describes two representative events that he personally experienced on his first day in New York: the cheerful experience of joining the lively Christmas shopping atmosphere, 「夕方、買い物をするために町へ行った。... 両親にペアの時計を買ってあげることにした。」 (“In the evening, I went into town to shop … I decided to buy my parents a matching pair of watches”), and the frightening experience of witnessing a woman fall and lose all her belongings, 「帰り道、ビルの狭い入口に人が四、五人集まっていた。その中には、女の人が倒れていて... 私は少し怖くなった。」 (“On the way back, four or five people had gathered at the narrow entrance of a building. Among them, a woman had fallen … I became a little frightened”). The message is summarized clearly at the end: 「アメリカに来たばかりなので、分からないところがいろいろあると思います。でも、いろいろ見たり聞いたりして、アメリカ社会を体験して行こうと思います。」 (“Since I have only just arrived in America, I think there are many things I do not understand. But I intend to see and hear various things and gradually experience American society.”) The key N3 grammar is 「V-たばかり」 (the verb in ta-form), meaning “have just done something” according to the speaker’s subjective sense of recency, and 「V-ていく」 (here in the volitional form, て行こう), expressing a determination to begin now and continue into the future while exploring. In reading questions based on letters (手紙文), do not be distracted by a single dramatic incident, such as the one in choice (c), or by minor details in choices (a) and (d). default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t2-p1.vietnamese:
The word “NEET” is said to have originated in the United Kingdom. In short, it is a word describing young people who do not work and have not received education or vocational training; in Europe and elsewhere, they had become a major social problem. In Japan as well, the existence of NEETs who are completely without work has recently begun to attract attention, and the government has also started working to support their independence.

For example, the national and prefectural governments invested a great deal of money to establish “job cafés,” promoting a stylish atmosphere suited to young people and free internet as their selling points. However, as a survey result shows, 98.8% of NEETs have never used a NEET support facility, so the youth employment measures, despite an investment of 76.1 billion yen, have not produced much effect.

There is also concern that, if things continue this way, a “poor class” may emerge in Japan, so prompt and effective measures are desired.

(Note) Job café: Here, the term refers to a workplace established for NEETs.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.sentences.0: Even in the past, some people with a talent for drawing made beautiful New Year’s cards using prints or drawings, but most people made cards with much the same content and designs.

Describes a past activity or habit, here how people used to make cards.
Contrasts two statements: some made beautiful cards, but most made similar ones.
Modifies a noun with the meaning “like” or “similar”; 同じような does not necessarily mean identical.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.sentences.2: But with computers and printers becoming widespread, people became able to offer New Year’s greetings through cards that reflected their own sensibilities and tastes.

Question 2: the cultural practice is making cards for New Year’s greetings. Question 3: this concrete benefit illustrates the role of computers in everyday life.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.sentences.3: Even without a talent for drawing or with poor handwriting, computers and printers help conceal ①one’s weaknesses through cheerful pictorial symbols and designs, beautiful lettering, and similar features.

Question 3: concealing personal limitations is a concrete example of how computers benefit everyday life.

Expresses the writer’s conjecture, “probably,” rather than a claim based on numerical evidence.
Question 1: restates the limitations mentioned in the preceding sentence, reinforcing option 2, poor handwriting.
Question 3: computers also relieve feelings of inferiority, further supporting their positive role in everyday life.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.sentences.5: Computers are said to have changed Japanese culture, but this can be seen as one example showing that they also contribute to carrying cultural traditions forward.

A written-style conclusion meaning “one could say…” いえよう is the volitional form of the potential いえる, used here to present a judgment.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.outline.0.l: New Year’s cards in the past
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.outline.0.n: Some talented people made beautiful cards, but most produced similar ones that could seem insincere. Making these cards establishes the cultural practice referred to at the end.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.outline.1.n: Widespread access to computers and printers enables people to express their own sensibilities and tastes through New Year’s cards.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.outline.2.n: Attractive images, designs, and lettering help people with limited drawing ability or poor handwriting make cards without revealing those limitations. Among the choices for question 1, poor handwriting is explicitly mentioned.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.outline.3.n: The writer concludes that computers also help sustain the tradition of making New Year’s cards. This example illustrates their important role in everyday life.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t3-p1.vietnamese:
Even in the past, some people with a talent for drawing made beautiful New Year’s cards using prints or drawings, but most people made cards with much the same content and designs. With cards like these, it is hardly surprising if people say they lack sincerity. But with computers and printers becoming widespread, people became able to offer New Year’s greetings through cards that reflected their own sensibilities and tastes. Even without a talent for drawing or with poor handwriting, computers and printers help conceal one’s weaknesses through cheerful pictorial symbols and designs, beautiful lettering, and similar features. Many people probably feel that computers and printers have freed them from feelings of inferiority such as “I cannot draw” or “My handwriting is poor.”

Computers are said to have changed Japanese culture, but this can be seen as one example showing that they also contribute to carrying cultural traditions forward.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t4-p1.sentences.0: The “priority seats” now found on trains and buses used to be called “①silver seats.”

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t4-p1.sentences.2: Turning to another issue, one often hears debate about whether these “priority seats” are really necessary and whether their very existence might actually be causing ②people’s moral standards to decline.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t4-p1.outline.0.l: The former name and why it changed

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t4-p1.outline.1.l: Questioning the effect of priority seats

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t4-p1.vietnamese:
The “priority seats” now found on trains and buses used to be called “①silver seats.” The name was chosen because “silver” refers to people with silver-colored hair, that is, older people. Later, however, it came to be recognized that older people could not be the only ones who should be offered a seat, so the name changed to “priority seats.”

Turning to another issue, one often hears debate about whether these “priority seats” are really necessary and whether their very existence might actually be causing ②people’s moral standards to decline. To begin with, when healthy people see an older person or someone with a physical disability, immediately offering their seat should be a matter of course. Yet the concern is that specially setting up “priority seats” and urging people to “Please offer your seat” might imply that healthy people sitting in ordinary seats do not need to give them up.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.outline.0.n: Introduces the culture of giving gifts or money for celebrations (weddings, childbirths, school admissions), hospital visits, and thank-you gifts before Obon and at year-end.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.l: Modern gift-giving occasions and bustling shopping
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.n: Describes the newer trend of giving presents on holidays like Mother's Day, Father's Day, Christmas, and Valentine's Day, packing department store gift counters.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.outline.2.l: The role of letters and seasonal greeting postcards
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.outline.2.n: Highlights the role of letters in Japanese life through sending summer greeting cards (Shochumimai) in late July and New Year's cards (Nengajo) in large numbers.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese:
In Japan, people often give gifts to one another. They present goods or money for celebratory events such as weddings, childbirths, and school admissions, or to visit the sick. Furthermore, before the Obon festival and at the end of the year, people send groceries and daily necessities to express their heartfelt gratitude to those who regularly look after them.

Moreover, in recent years, people have also come to give presents on various other occasions besides these. Examples include 'Mother's Day' in May, 'Father's Day' in June, along with Christmas in December and Valentine's Day in February. During these seasons, gift sections in department stores everywhere become packed with shoppers.

Letters also play an important role in the daily lives of Japanese people. In late July and during the New Year period, people send postcards to friends and acquaintances. Postcards sent in July are called 'Shochumimai' (summer greeting cards), while those sent for the New Year are called 'Nengajo' (New Year's cards). In particular, there are individuals who mail hundreds of New Year's cards all by themselves.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t6-p1.sentences.0: You know what kind of day Christmas is, don't you?

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t6-p1.outline.1.n: Moves from gifts to Valentine's Day: women give chocolate to men to express affection, and even elementary school pupils participate.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t6-p1.outline.2.n: Introduces chocolate associated with social courtesy and workplace gratitude rather than romantic confession. This supports option 1 for question 1.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t6-p1.outline.4.n: Ends with a mildly ironic comment about confectioners' commercial influence. Question 3 requires synthesizing the examples of festive participation; the passage does not describe a deliberate intention to help manufacturers.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t6-p1.vietnamese:
You know what kind of day Christmas is, don't you? In Japan, many people exchange gifts on this day, regardless of religion: between romantic partners, from parents to their young children, and among friends.

Speaking of gifts, there is Valentine's Day (February 14). In Japan, women give chocolate to men to express their love. Even elementary school girls give it to the boy they like. However, there is also chocolate that the recipient cannot feel entirely happy about. This is called obligation chocolate; women may, for example, discreetly give it to their superiors at work. It is not a declaration of love, but probably a token of thanks for the help received each day.

Those who received chocolate give a return gift on March 14. Perhaps because people give white things, such as white chocolate, in return, that day is called White Day.

Both Christmas and Valentine's Day somehow leave us feeling that we have been swept along by the commercialism of confectionery shops, don't they?

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.1: This is because they must always listen to other people's opinions.
not listening; part of an obligation construction
Expresses obligation: must do something. Attach なくてはいけない to the negative stem; 聞く becomes 聞かなくてはいけない.
Means 'this is because...'; explains the preceding statement in a formal written style.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.2: They also want to attract attention by talking with various people, appearing on television, and being written about in newspapers.
Lists representative activities without making the list exhaustive.
Passive forms: 書かれる means 'be written about'; 注目される means 'receive attention'.
Expresses an ongoing desire or intention: wants to...
話し is the continuative form of 話す, linking actions in writing; it is not the reason-listing particle し.
Helps rule out question 1, option 1: the text describes a desire for attention, not a prohibition against attracting it.
Helps rule out question 3, option 1: television appearances are listed as an example, with no claim that they happen frequently.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.3: However, receiving attention alone is not enough.
Means '... alone is not enough'; something further is required.
A formal written equivalent of だ.
For question 1, this limits the value of attention and introduces the duty to work for supporters; it does not prohibit receiving attention.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.4: They must work for the people who support them.
not doing; part of an obligation construction
Marks an action benefiting the speaker or viewpoint holder; here, supporting the politician.
Means 'for the benefit of...'; here, for those people.
Directly supports question 1, option 4: politicians must work for the benefit of their supporters.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.5: For example, they must bring in new business to improve the economy or improve schools.
not doing; part of an obligation construction
Expresses a desired outcome: so that the economy improves.
An i-adjective stem plus くなる means 'become...'; plus くする means 'make...'. よくなる means 'improve'; よくする means 'make better'.
Lists representative activities that must be carried out.
Illustrates question 1, option 4, with actions that benefit the community.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.6: If they do not do a good job, that politician's reputation will suffer, and they will probably be called unreliable (note 1).
Means 'if ... not'; this is a negative condition, not the obligation pattern ～なければならない.
The continuative form of ～くなる, describing a change and connecting to the next clause.
Means 'will probably be called...'; と marks the quoted judgment, いわれる is passive, and だろう expresses prediction.
For question 1, this describes the consequences of poor work and reinforces option 4; it does not support option 2's claim that politicians must not care about their reputation.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.7: Artists are a different type of person from politicians.
Means 'different from...'; と marks the comparison target.
A formal written structure identifying or introducing something: ... is...
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.8: Many artists have a distinctive individuality.
Describes a common characteristic in a group without claiming it applies to every member.
Supports question 2, option 2: artists often have a distinctive individuality.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.9: Among them, some are stubborn and inflexible (note 2).
Means 'among them, there are also some who...'; limits the statement to a subset.
The connective form of a na-adjective: 頑固で links stubbornness with inflexibility.
Rules out question 3, option 4: only some artists are described as inflexible, not artists as a whole.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.sentences.1: However, in an artist's work, their own ideas matter more than what others say, so it is acceptable to be stubborn.
Compares two things: B is more ... than A. Here, one's own ideas matter more than others' words.
Means 'because...'; gives the reason stubbornness is acceptable.
Means 'it is acceptable even if...'. With a na-adjective, use its stem plus でもかまわない: 頑固でもかまわない.
Directly supports question 2, option 2: artists place importance on their own ideas.
If they listen too much to other people's opinions, they will end up becoming ordinary artists.
Expresses excess; attach すぎる to the masu-stem. 聞きすぎる means 'listen too much'.
Introduces a consequence the author presents as naturally following a condition.
Means 'end up becoming...'; ～てしまう emphasizes an undesirable outcome here.
Reinforces question 2, option 2: excessive reliance on others' opinions undermines individuality, making personal ideas important.
And the works created by ordinary artists are not very interesting.
not very; used with a negative
In a noun-modifying clause, の can replace が as the subject marker: 芸術家の作ったもの means 'things the artist created'.
Means 'not very...' or 'not much...'; indicates a low degree.
(Note 2) Inflexible: being rigid in one's thinking and lacking flexibility.
The connective form of an i-adjective: 固い becomes 固くて, linking two characteristics in the definition.
Expresses absence: 柔軟性がない means 'lack flexibility'.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.outline.0.n: Politicians tend to be sociable because they must listen to others; they also seek public attention. Distinguish a common trait from a requirement, and an example activity from its frequency.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.outline.1.n: Attention alone is insufficient: politicians must work for their supporters, for example by improving the economy and schools. Poor performance damages their reputation.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.outline.2.n: The passage shifts to artists as a contrast to politicians. Artists often have distinctive personalities; only some are stubborn and inflexible.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.outline.3.n: In artistic work, personal ideas matter more than others' words. Listening too much to others leads to ordinariness and less interesting work.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.outline.4.n: Defines the expressions for being unreliable and inflexible.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t7-p1.vietnamese:
Most politicians tend to be sociable people. This is because they must always listen to other people's opinions. They also want to attract attention by talking with various people, appearing on television, and being written about in newspapers. However, receiving attention alone is not enough. They must work for the people who support them. For example, they must bring in new business to improve the economy or improve schools. If they do not do a good job, that politician's reputation will suffer, and they will probably be called unreliable (note 1).

Artists are a different type of person from politicians. Many artists have a distinctive individuality. Among them, some are stubborn and inflexible (note 2). However, in an artist's work, their own ideas matter more than what others say, so it is acceptable to be stubborn. If they listen too much to other people's opinions, they will end up becoming ordinary artists. And the works created by ordinary artists are not very interesting.

(Note 1) Unreliable: cannot be depended on.

(Note 2) Inflexible: being rigid in one's thinking and lacking flexibility.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.0: The other day, when I attended an earthquake preparedness drill, the host announced, “Our ‘sensei’ is here and will say a few words.”
sensei, an honorific used here for a politician
When something happened; 参加した時 sets the time of the incident.
Gives a reason: the guest is present, so there will be some remarks.
There was a statement that…; と marks the quotation and の connects it to 発言.
An honorific expression for coming or being present; here it means the guest has arrived and is present.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.1: As I wondered who it could be, it turned out to be a local city council member.
Expresses wondering to oneself: I wonder…
While thinking or wondering, the speaker discovers something.
Question 1: identifies the person described in the next sentence as a city council member; option 4.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.2: I did think, “They seem to be working very hard” (①, note 1), but I could not feel particularly favorable toward them.
with all one's effort; very hard
seem to be doing (as defined in note 1)
not very; not particularly (with a negative)
I did think… but…; は emphasizes a concession before a contrasting judgment.
Not very…; indicates a low degree.
Cannot do something; here, cannot feel favorably toward someone.
Expresses a personal impression or a thought to oneself.
Question 1: this is the author's impression of the council member just introduced, rather than a description of the author.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.3: During the general election, a newly elected legislator said, “I want to be someone who is not called ‘sensei,’ someone people can comfortably talk to about anything.”
can receive an action from someone
want to be; want to remain
Not be called…; 言われる is the passive form of 言う.
Can have someone do something for one; here, have people talk comfortably to the legislator.
The kind of person who…; the preceding clause describes the desired qualities.
Want to be or remain…; used with a noun describing a role or state.
Stated that…; reports the content of someone's words.
Question 3: shows that humility here means being approachable so people can talk freely to the person; option 2.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.4: I believe that legislators are representatives of the people.
A person whose role or nature is…; here it identifies the role of representing the people.
I believe that this is what something is; なのだ adds an explanatory emphasis.
Question 2: the direct basis is that legislators represent the people; option 3.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.5: I think we should stop using the title “sensei” for them (②).
