The way of addressing someone as…; specifies the title under discussion.
Should do something; やめたほうがいい means it would be better to stop, not that stopping has already happened.
I think that…; expresses a personal opinion.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.6: Even if people initially intend to be humble (③), human beings are susceptible to weakness.
even if one thinks or intends
Even if one thinks or intends…; introduces a concession.
An elliptical expression, understood as 謙虚にしようと: intending to behave humbly.
Question 3: places humility in the person's initial intention; compare sentence 3's wish to be approachable with sentence 7's condescending attitude.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.7: If people keep being called “sensei, sensei,” they tend to develop a condescending attitude toward others (note 2), and an equal relationship gradually becomes impossible to maintain.
If something continues…; a verb stem plus 続ける in the conditional ば form.
Come to no longer…; 保たれなくなる means to cease being maintained.
Describes a change that develops gradually over time.
Presents something as a general tendency or characteristic in the speaker's view.
Question 2: supports the objection to the title by explaining that it can undermine equality between representatives and the people.
Question 3: a condescending attitude is the opposite of humility, ruling out option 4 and supporting approachability.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.8: (Note 1) やってみえる: to appear to be doing something.
Appear to be doing something; this is how the note defines やってみえる in this passage.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.sentences.9: (Note 2) 目線: normally means one's line of sight, but here it means perspective or attitude.
Is… but…; contrasts the usual meaning with the contextual meaning.
Means…; explains what an expression refers to.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.0.l: An experience at a preparedness drill
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.0.n: The author hears the host call a city council member “sensei.” Although the member seems hardworking, the author does not feel particularly favorable toward them.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.1.n: A new legislator wants people to speak freely without calling them “sensei.” The author states that legislators represent the people.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.2.l: Dropping the title to preserve equality
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.2.n: The author advocates dropping “sensei”: even an initially humble person may become condescending when repeatedly addressed by this title, undermining an equal relationship.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.outline.3.n: Explains that やってみえる means appearing to do something, and that 目線 here refers to perspective or attitude.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t9-p1.vietnamese:
The other day, when I attended an earthquake preparedness drill, the host announced, “Our ‘sensei’ is here and will say a few words.” As I wondered who it could be, it turned out to be a local city council member. I did think, “①They seem to be working very hard” (note 1), but I could not feel particularly favorable toward them.

During the general election, a newly elected legislator said, “I want to be someone who is not called ‘sensei,’ someone people can comfortably talk to about anything.” I believe that legislators are representatives of the people.

②I think we should stop using the title “sensei” for them. Even if people initially intend to be ③humble, human beings are susceptible to weakness. If people keep being called “sensei, sensei,” they tend to develop a condescending attitude toward others (note 2), and an equal relationship gradually becomes impossible to maintain.

(Note 1) やってみえる: to appear to be doing something.

(Note 2) 目線: normally means one's line of sight, but here it means perspective or attitude.
Meeting the actor I admired felt like a dream, and I was deeply moved.
Highlights something with surprise or strong emotion: actually getting to meet the actor.
Expresses an impression or comparison: as if dreaming. ようで connects this impression to the next clause.
会える is the potential form of 会う: to be able to meet or get to meet.
But later, hearing a friend tell me about a television drama made me reflect.
Means to hear something from someone; 友だちから identifies the friend as the source.
The causative passive; here it means that the story prompted the narrator to reflect.

The girl who was the main character had no idea that the wonderful star had secretly undergone cosmetic surgery; simply because she wanted to look just like that person, she secretly had an operation to make her face look slimmer without telling her parents.
had performed or applied; here, had had cosmetic work done
Describes something that had already happened before the time being discussed: the star had already had surgery.
こと turns a clause into the object of 知らない: not know that something is the case.
Emphasizes a complete negative: not know at all.
A negative linking form similar to ～ないで; 知らず means without knowing.
Expresses a strong desire as the cause of an undesirable result: simply because someone wanted to do something.
Means to keep something secret from someone.
Means to make something look a certain way; 顔を細く見せる means to make the face look slimmer.
A conversational expression that explains or emphasizes what happened.
The main evidence for question 1, option 1: the star had already had cosmetic surgery, but the girl did not know.
Explains the irony: the girl wanted to look exactly like her idol without knowing that the idol's appearance had been surgically altered.
She became noticeably prettier, but I somehow felt, “Isn't that an ironic story?”
had, in an expression of feeling
Expresses a change of state: became prettier.
Connects contrasting ideas: she became prettier, yet the story felt ironic.
A question seeking agreement: isn't it…? It does not deny that the story is ironic.
Expresses the speaker's impression: I had the feeling that…
For question 1, the girl did become prettier, which rules out option 4.
The expression in question 1 refers back to the star's surgery, which the girl knew nothing about.
The girl was shocked at how expensive the operation was; her pocket money was nowhere near enough.
height; here, how high the cost was
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing degree: 高い → 高さ, height or how high a price is.
Means to be surprised at something; に marks the cause of surprise.
Means that the specified amount or financial resource is insufficient.
Emphasizes a negative: not enough at all.
So she suddenly tried to earn money for the operation by selling her own blood.
did; part of an expression of intention or attempt
The て-form expresses the means: earning money by selling blood.
The volitional form followed by とした expresses an intention or attempt; 稼ごう is the volitional form of 稼ぐ.
Explains the course of events in a conversational tone.
Direct evidence for question 2, option 4: そこ refers to events up to selling blood to pay for surgery.
Well, even if we let things pass up to that point, what happened afterward was another matter…
Marks a limit and sets up a contrast: up to that point…
Provisionally accepts or sets aside one issue before moving to the next; として here does not mean “in the capacity of.”
A trailing expression after が that hints at a problem; ね adds a conversational, shared tone.
For question 2, そこ points back to selling blood in the preceding sentence, which the friend sets aside before discussing the consequences.
The poor girl became infected through a needle and, shockingly, ended up becoming an AIDS patient.
から marks the source or route of infection described in the story: a needle.
Expresses a completed outcome with regret or distress.
A conversational ending that adds explanation and emphasis.
For question 3, this tragic outcome supports the friend's caution against having surgery for beauty in this story.
It really is a pitiful story.
Expresses emotion and invites the listener's sympathy or agreement.
For question 3, this expresses pity and helps establish the friend's cautionary tone.
Even admiration for a star needs to be kept within reasonable limits.
not do; here, part of a reminder to exercise moderation
Indicates the target of a feeling: admiration for a star.
Means to bring or keep something in a state; ほどほどにする means to keep it moderate.
An abbreviated form of ～ないといけない that gently states a necessity: one needs to exercise moderation.

The main evidence for question 3, option 1: in context, the call for moderation implies that one should not have surgery merely to look as beautiful as an idol. This is an inference, not an explicit ban on surgery.
My friend told me all this with deep feeling.
Describes someone doing something for or toward the speaker; here, the friend told the narrator the story.
Identifies the friend as the person giving the preceding comments and advice; しみじみ conveys deep feeling.
(Note 1) 内緒: here, this means not telling one's parents that one wants to have cosmetic surgery.
want to do; want to undergo
Expresses a desire to perform an action: wanting to have surgery.
Nominalizes clauses: wanting surgery and not telling one's parents.
Explains what a word refers to in context.
(Note 2) ほどほど: a moderate degree that does not involve overdoing things or going beyond reasonable limits.
Expresses doing something excessively; やりすぎる means to overdo something.
Lists representative actions. しない negates the list: neither overdoing things nor going beyond limits.
Expresses a degree or extent, modified by the preceding clause.
Supports question 3 by confirming that ほどほど means avoiding excess, clarifying the advice to keep admiration within limits.
The narrator feels moved after meeting an admired actor, then is prompted to reflect by a friend's account of a drama.
The girl has surgery to resemble her idol without knowing that the idol has also had surgery. She becomes prettier, but the situation is described as ironic.
Selling blood to pay for surgery
Her pocket money is insufficient, so the girl tries to sell blood. そこ in the next sentence refers to events up to this action.
Consequences and a call for moderation
The story ends with a tragic consequence and advice against excessive admiration. Among the choices in question 3, option 1 matches this cautionary message.
Explains 内緒 as keeping the desire for surgery secret from one's parents and ほどほど as staying within reasonable limits.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t10-p1.vietnamese:
Meeting the actor I admired felt like a dream, and I was deeply moved. But later, hearing a friend tell me about a television drama made me reflect. The girl who was the main character had no idea that the wonderful star had secretly undergone cosmetic surgery; simply because she wanted to look just like that person, she secretly had an operation to make her face look slimmer without telling her parents. She became noticeably prettier, but I somehow felt, “Isn't that an ironic story?” The girl was shocked at how expensive the operation was; her pocket money was nowhere near enough. So she suddenly tried to earn money for the operation by selling her own blood. Well, even if we let things pass up to that point, what happened afterward was another matter… The poor girl became infected through a needle and, shockingly, ended up becoming an AIDS patient. It really is a pitiful story. Even admiration for a star needs to be kept within reasonable limits. My friend told me all this with deep feeling.

(Note 1) 内緒: here, this means not telling one's parents that one wants to have cosmetic surgery.

(Note 2) ほどほど: a moderate degree that does not involve overdoing things or going beyond reasonable limits.
There is a view that Japan's economy has been improving because Japanese salaried workers work hard.
Expresses a change developing up to the present: the economy has gradually improved.
Explains a cause: the reason that… is because…; である is a formal written form.
There is a view that…; introduces an opinion without necessarily presenting it as the author's conclusion.
Certainly, it is possible to do such a thing.
Here, そういうこと is a noun phrase meaning “such a thing,” followed by ができる to express ability. The original does not say そう言うことができる, “can say so.”
However, it can also be said that Japanese salaried workers have little time for themselves.
Identifies who lacks something; は highlights the group under discussion.
Not much; expresses a low degree rather than necessarily a complete absence.
It can also be said that…; adds another perspective.
Question 3: directly states the lack of personal time underlying the author's sympathetic view of young workers.
For example, reportedly, some young salaried workers ①have no time to date.
Among… there are people who…; does not describe every member of the group.
People who have no time to…; の replaces が within the clause modifying 人.
Reportedly…; a plain form followed by そうである conveys hearsay, not an inference from appearance.
Question 1: identifies the people being asked about. Question 3: illustrates their lack of personal time through having no time to date.
A formal written copula corresponding to だ or です.
Question 3: calling the lack of time to date a major concern supports the author's sympathetic attitude.
That is why companies that introduce potential dating partners seem to have become popular recently.
Describes someone doing something beneficial for the viewpoint holder; here, introducing dating partners for clients.
In 流行っている, describes the current state of being popular.
It seems that…; presents a tentative judgment based on circumstances.
Question 1: these companies provide introductions to dating partners; the passage does not say young people work for them as option 2 suggests.
Marriage through matchmaking has long existed in Japan (see note), but using companies like these could perhaps be called a new way of matchmaking.
Connects contrasting clauses: traditional matchmaking and a new method.
の nominalizes こんな会社を使う, and は makes “using companies like these” the topic.
Could perhaps be described as…; combines a possible characterization with uncertainty.
Question 1: using a dating introduction company is described as a new form of matchmaking, matching option 3. The passage does not state that they have married.
In addition, they have little time to enjoy sports.
Not only… but also…; adds the lack of time for sports to the lack of time for dating.
Not much…; emphasizes the limited time available for sports.
A dictionary-form verb modifies 時間: time to do something.
Question 3: gives another example of limited personal time, contradicting option 3's claim that they are enjoying their hobbies.
Even people who liked sports as students may gain weight and end up losing some of their physical coordination.
When one was…; 学生の時 refers to one's student days.
Here means “even,” emphasizing that former sports enthusiasts may also be affected.
An い-adjective changes to its ～く form before なる to express a change of state.
Expresses an undesirable outcome with a sense of regret.
May; might…; expresses a possibility, not a confirmed fact about many people.
Question 3: this is a possible consequence of lacking time for exercise. かもしれない does not establish that many people are overweight, as option 4 claims.
Once things reach this point, enjoying hobbies and the like becomes ②a distant, unattainable dream, and the year slips away in trips back and forth between their apartment and the office.
going back and forth; round trip
When/if… then…; こうなると introduces the consequence of the preceding situation.
Gives an example, “things such as…”; here emphasizes how out of reach enjoying hobbies is.
で after 夢のまた夢 is the connective form of だ, linking this description to the following clause.
In 往復で1年が終わる, で marks the activity that fills the period: the year passes in commuting.
Emphasizes that the whole year passes, with regret over the lack of personal time.
Question 2: the idiom describes something so remote that it is virtually impossible to achieve; option 4 is the intended match. It does not refer to dreams during sleep.
Question 3: spending the entire year going between home and work conveys a lack of personal time and the author's sympathy.
Their life after retirement is a cause for concern.
Be concerned about…; expresses the author's worry about life after retirement.
Question 3: the closing concern reinforces the author's sympathy for their lack of personal time, supporting option 2.
(Note) Marriage through matchmaking: getting acquainted through an intermediary and then marrying.
Through…; identifies an intermediary or medium.
Links actions in sequence: becoming acquainted and then marrying.
Nominalizes the action to define 見合い結婚.
Hard work and little personal time
Introduces a view about workers' contribution to the economy, then uses しかし to turn to the main issue: their limited personal time.
No time to date and a new form of matchmaking
Some young workers have no time to date. Introduction services become popular, and using them is described as a new form of matchmaking, supporting option 3 for question 1.
Unattainable hobbies and concern for the future
Limited time for sports may affect physical fitness. Enjoying hobbies becomes 夢のまた夢 while the year passes in commuting. The ending conveys the author's concern and sympathy.
Defines 見合い結婚 as becoming acquainted through an intermediary and then marrying; this is a vocabulary note.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t12-p1.vietnamese:
There is a view that Japan's economy has been improving because Japanese salaried workers work hard. Certainly, it is possible to do such a thing. However, it can also be said that Japanese salaried workers have little time for themselves.

For example, reportedly, some young salaried workers ①have no time to date. This is a major concern. That is why companies that introduce potential dating partners seem to have become popular recently. Marriage through matchmaking has long existed in Japan (see note), but using companies like these could perhaps be called a new way of matchmaking.

In addition, they have little time to enjoy sports. Even people who liked sports as students may gain weight and end up losing some of their physical coordination. Once things reach this point, enjoying hobbies and the like becomes ②a distant, unattainable dream, and the year slips away in trips back and forth between their apartment and the office. Their life after retirement is a cause for concern.

(Note) Marriage through matchmaking: getting acquainted through an intermediary and then marrying.
When Obon arrives, Bon dances are held in various places.
when something becomes or reaches a certain time
Until now, I had only made a brief appearance at neighborhood association activities.
to the extent of; only about
This year, because it became my turn to be in charge of the neighborhood association, I participated thoroughly from preparation through cleanup.
The area where I live is a new residential district, so my relationships with the neighbors consist only of greetings, and almost everyone is a stranger to me.
I thought that this was probably all there was to men's relationships with their neighbors, and until then I think I had little interest in my neighborhood or community.
such as; expressing dismissal or devaluation
However, mutual assistance in the local community becomes important during natural disasters and similar situations.
This sentence directly states that community cooperation becomes important during natural disasters, matching the situation asked about.
As I watched the small children innocently running around at the Bon dance festival, I thought that I had to pay more attention not only to my company and family but also to the community.
The writer realizes that he must pay more attention to the community, showing a change in his view of involvement with the neighborhood.
Taking my participation in this Bon dance festival as an opportunity, I decided that from now on I would talk with my neighbors more than before and remember their faces as well.
participation in the Bon dance festival
will remember their faces as well
more than; to a greater extent than
This phrase shows that participating in the festival became the opportunity that led to a change in the writer's thoughts and actions.
The writer decides to talk with neighbors and remember their faces, showing an awareness of the importance of neighborhood relationships.
(Note 1) Obon: one of Japan's traditional events, an activity of praying for deceased people.
(Note 2) Neighborhood association: a residents' organization formed in an urban neighborhood.
(Note 3) Innocently: in a charming, childlike manner.
The writer introduces the Bon dance festival and explains how his involvement grew from briefly showing up to participating fully after being assigned responsibility.
Because he lives in a new residential district, the writer barely knows his neighbors and previously had little interest in the community.
The writer realizes that mutual assistance is important during natural disasters, leading him to pay more attention to the community and become more involved with neighbors.
The notes explain the meanings of お盆, 町内会, and 無邪気に.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t13-p1.vietnamese:
When Obon arrives, Bon dances are held in various places. Until now, I had only made a brief appearance at neighborhood association activities. This year, because it became my turn to be in charge of the neighborhood association, I participated thoroughly from preparation through cleanup.

The area where I live is a new residential district, so my relationships with the neighbors consist only of greetings, and almost everyone is a stranger to me. I thought that this was probably all there was to men's relationships with their neighbors, and until then I think I had little interest in my neighborhood or community.

However, mutual assistance in the local community becomes important during natural disasters and similar situations. As I watched the small children innocently running around at the Bon dance festival, I thought that I had to pay more attention not only to my company and family but also to the community. Taking my participation in this Bon dance festival as an opportunity, I decided that from now on I would talk with my neighbors more than before and remember their faces as well.

(Note 1) Obon: one of Japan's traditional events, an activity of praying for deceased people.

(Note 2) Neighborhood association: a residents' organization formed in an urban neighborhood.

(Note 3) Innocently: in a charming, childlike manner.
My eldest son, a first-year high school student, came home somewhat late in the evening.
An i-adjective changes to ～く to modify a verb: 遅く帰宅した means came home late.
I was already in bed, but my eldest daughter, a first-year junior high school student, was still awake.
Describes an ongoing state at a past time: being in bed or remaining awake.
Connects contrasting clauses: the narrator was in bed, while the daughter was still awake.
As soon as my eldest son opened the front door, he called to his younger sister, who had been staying in her room, “Come here a moment,” and went outside again.
eldest daughter; the younger sister in the story
Indicates that the second event follows immediately after the first: upon opening the door, he called to his sister.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: 部屋にこもっていた describes 長女.
来い is the imperative of 来る, with a direct, informal tone; here it is the brother calling his sister.
Uses と to quote the words spoken when calling out to someone.
声をかけ is the continuative form of 声をかける, linking the call to the following action.
Describes something that keeps occurring without cease; here, the siblings' frequent quarrels.
The sentence ends with the noun 二人, omitting a predicate to highlight the constantly bickering pair.
Supporting context for Question 1: the siblings habitually quarrel.
That day, too, they had just had an argument.
did; had an argument in this phrase
Means having just done something. したばかり shows that the argument had only recently occurred.
Means “too”: they argued that day as they had on other occasions.
Direct evidence for Question 1, option 1: she ignored him because they had just argued.
①At first, my daughter ignored him, but after a little while she seemed to go outside through the front entrance.
eldest daughter; the younger sister in the story
Presents an initial state followed by a contrasting development: she first ignored him but later went outside.
The formal past form of ～ようだ, expressing “seemed to” based on what the narrator perceived.
That night was the night of the celebrated mid-autumn moon.
A noun-predicate sentence with だ omitted, briefly establishing the mid-autumn setting.
Having seen the remarkably beautiful moon on his way home, my son apparently wanted to share it with someone, so he invited his younger sister outside.
want to convey; want to share
eldest daughter; the younger sister in the story
The clause あまりに美しい月を帰り道で見た modifies 長男: the son who saw the beautiful moon on his way home.
Means “apparently wanted to”; ようで links the inferred desire to his invitation.
An explanatory narrative ending that clarifies the reason behind an earlier action.
Evidence for Question 2, option 4: the brother appreciated the beauty of the moon.
Direct evidence for Question 3, option 3: それ refers to the beautiful moon, which he wanted his sister to see too.
When we encounter a beautiful sight, we feel like sharing it with someone.
Expresses a natural response: encountering beauty leads to a desire to share it.
Means coming to want to do something or developing an urge to act.
Supports Questions 2 and 3: appreciating a beautiful sight prompts a desire to share it, explaining the invitation.
That desire is even stronger when it is someone close to us.
Introduces a case: if the person to share with is someone close.
Means “all the more so in that case”; the omitted idea is an even stronger desire to share the beautiful sight.
This feeling that wells up naturally is perhaps something unique to human beings.
Expresses a quality unique to something. 人ならではのもの means something distinctive to human beings.
Expresses the narrator's supposition: probably or perhaps.

Imagining my son that night standing beside the sister he was always arguing with and gazing at the full moon, I felt a warmth in my heart and was reassured: “②His emotional sensitivity is developing well.”
eldest daughter; the younger sister in the story
Attaches to a verb stem to express a reciprocal action: けんかし合う means quarrel with each other.
In 想像すると, と links imagining the scene with the warm feeling it produces.
Means to experience a particular feeling; あったかい気持ちになる means to feel warmth in one's heart.
な adds a reflective, emotional tone, while と introduces the thought that reassures the narrator.
A narrative ending emphasizing the narrator's concluding explanation or feeling.
The context for Question 2 is moon viewing; together with sentence 7, it identifies 情緒 as sensitivity to the moon's beauty.
Question 2 takes option 4: the narrator is reassured by the son's sensitivity to beauty, shown in his appreciation of the moon.
Note: “Unique to human beings” means “distinctively human.”
Marks a characteristic unique to the preceding noun; here it is glossed as 人特有の.
The brother comes home and calls his sister
Introduces the siblings and the narrator. The brother comes home somewhat late, calls his sister from her room, and goes outside again.
A recent argument explains her initial silence
The siblings often quarrel and had just argued that day. This explains why the sister initially ignored her brother.
The beautiful moon explains the invitation
The brother saw the beautiful moon on his way home and invited his sister to share the sight. This also shows his sensitivity to beauty.
The narrator reflects on the natural desire to share beautiful sights, especially with someone close.
Reassurance about the son's emotional growth
Imagining the siblings viewing the moon together warms the narrator's heart and reassures them about the son's emotional development. A final note explains 人ならではの.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
My eldest son, a first-year high school student, came home somewhat late in the evening. I was already in bed, but my eldest daughter, a first-year junior high school student, was still awake. As soon as my son opened the front door, he called to his younger sister, who had been staying in her room, “Come here a moment,” and went outside again.

The two were always bickering. That day, too, they had just had an argument. ①At first, my daughter ignored him, but after a little while she seemed to go outside through the front entrance.

That night was the night of the celebrated mid-autumn moon. Having seen the remarkably beautiful moon on his way home, my son apparently wanted to share it with someone, so he invited his younger sister outside.

When we encounter a beautiful sight, we feel like sharing it with someone. That desire is even stronger when it is someone close to us. This feeling that wells up naturally is perhaps something unique to human beings.

Imagining my son that night standing beside the sister he was always arguing with and gazing at the full moon, I felt a warmth in my heart and was reassured: “②His emotional sensitivity is developing well.”

Note: “Unique to human beings” means “distinctively human.”
As my memory has grown increasingly weaker, I often lose my sense of direction when I go somewhere else.
Describes a change developing up to the present: the speaker's memory has gradually weakened.
Expresses a condition with a habitual result: going somewhere else often leads to losing one's bearings.
Expresses a change to a state in which something is no longer true or possible.
After wandering around for hours, I end up having to get help from a police officer.
Introduces an often undesirable outcome after a prolonged process: wandering for hours and still needing help.
Expresses receiving a favor or assistance; 警察官に identifies the person providing help.
Here it conveys an unintended outcome with a sense of regret or helplessness.
After an interrogative quantity such as 何時間, emphasizes an extended amount: hours on end.
On reflection, perhaps this is less a matter of age and more that I have always had a poor sense of direction.
Introduces a realization after trying something; 考えてみると means 'on reflection.'
Identifies the cause of an unfavorable result: because of age.
Revises an explanation: B is more accurate than A. The speaker favors an existing poor sense of direction over age as the explanation.
Presents a possible explanation rather than a definite claim; nouns take ～なのかもしれない.
Question 1: option 3. The speaker sees an existing poor sense of direction as the more likely cause. ～かもしれない keeps the explanation tentative.
I envy people who can find their way to where they want to go using even a roughly drawn map.
A past passive form modifies a noun: 描かれた地図 means 'a map that was drawn.'
Means 'even': even a roughly drawn map can be used.
Means relying on someone or something to do something.
Expresses desire; 行きたい所 means a place one wants to go.
行ける is the potential form of 行く and expresses being able to reach a place.
When I simply cannot find the building I am heading for, I end up resenting the person who drew the map for me and cursing my own pathetic self.
Emphasizes that something remains impossible or does not happen despite one's efforts.
Presents a condition leading to a habitual reaction: failing to find the building leads to resentment.
Expresses someone having done something for the speaker: drawing a map for me.
Lists a representative action without making the list exhaustive; only 恨む takes ～たり in this sentence.
Means ending up with an undesirable result; here it does not describe a decision or rule.
Question 2: option 4. Failing to find the intended building frustrates the speaker and explains the need to calm down.
Once, thinking I should calm down first, I sat on a bench on a noisy street corner and took a short rest.
A volitional form followed by と思う expresses intention; 落ち着こう is the volitional form of 落ち着く.
Connects actions or circumstances: deciding to calm down, sitting down, and resting.
Then I plucked up the courage to ask a reliable-looking police officer (note 1) who was passing by, and he kindly gave me directions.
Describes an apparent quality: remove い from 頼もしい and add そうな to mean 'reliable-looking.'
Expresses trying an action: asking for directions.
Introduces a result discovered or obtained after an action: asking led to receiving helpful directions.
Describes someone doing something beneficial for the speaker, often with a sense of gratitude.
To my surprise, the building I had been looking for was right in front of me.
Describes an ongoing past action: the speaker had been searching for the building before asking.
Explains or emphasizes a realization; here it highlights the unexpected discovery.
Means having a particular feeling or experience; 恥ずかしい思いをする means 'feel embarrassed.'
However, ever since then, I have followed the principle, 'Ask rather than wander around lost.'
Marks the starting point of a continuing state or practice: ever since that occasion.
Compares two courses of action and favors one: asking rather than remaining lost.
聞け is the imperative form of 聞く. In this motto, it creates a short, forceful reminder: 'ask.'
Here it describes an ongoing practice: the speaker has adopted and continues to follow this principle.
Question 3: option 2. Since that experience, the speaker has made a practice of asking others when unsure of the way.
(Note 1) Reliable: someone or something one can count on and trust.
Combines with action nouns such as 期待 and 信用 to express possibility or ability.
The continuative form links clauses in writing: でき connects to the following clause, like できて.
The speaker describes a weakening memory, frequently losing direction away from familiar surroundings, and eventually needing police assistance.
The speaker considers an existing poor sense of direction more likely than age, envies capable map users, and becomes frustrated when unable to find the destination. Sentence 2 supports question 1; sentence 4 explains the need to calm down in question 2.
An occasion of asking for directions
The speaker rests to calm down, musters the courage to ask a police officer, and feels embarrassed on learning that the building is directly ahead.
Since that experience, the speaker has made a habit of asking for directions instead of continuing to wander lost. This directly supports question 3.
Defines 頼もしい as dependable and trustworthy, and はなはだ as extremely.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t15-p1.vietnamese:
As my memory has grown increasingly weaker, I often ①lose my sense of direction when I go somewhere else. After wandering around for hours, I end up having to get help from a police officer.

On reflection, perhaps this is less a matter of age and more that I have always had a poor sense of direction. I envy people who can find their way to where they want to go using even a roughly drawn map. When I simply cannot find the building I am heading for, I end up resenting the person who drew the map for me and cursing my own pathetic self. Once, ②thinking I should calm down first, I sat on a bench on a noisy street corner and took a short rest. Then I plucked up the courage to ask a reliable-looking police officer (note 1) who was passing by, and he kindly gave me directions. To my surprise, the building I had been looking for was right in front of me. I felt extremely (note 2) embarrassed.

However, ever since then, I have followed the principle, 'Ask rather than wander around lost.'

(Note 1) Reliable: someone or something one can count on and trust.

(Note 2) はなはだ: extremely; very.
Recently, I think children have been spending less time playing sports outdoors.
Describes a change continuing up to the present: 減ってきた means have been decreasing.
Expresses the speaker's opinion: I think that…
The preceding clause modifies 時間: the time children spend playing sports outdoors.
I think one reason that can be given is that there are fewer places where children can exercise.
Nominalizes a clause: 場所が減ったこと means the fact that available places have decreased.
Used to cite a reason or example: …can be given.
Question 1: directly states the cause, matching option 3. Fewer usable places does not necessarily mean fewer parks.
When I go to a park wanting to play soccer, there is a sign saying that soccer and playing catch (note 1) are prohibited.
wanting to play; wanting to do
if one goes; when one goes
The connective form of ～たい links a desire to the following action: going to a park because one wants to play soccer.
Expresses a condition; here it describes what one encounters when going to a park.
Introduces content or a name; 禁止という看板 is a sign stating a prohibition.
Lists examples without necessarily giving an exhaustive list.
When I go to another park, the grass (note 2) has grown too tall, stopping the ball and making it impossible to play.
if one goes; when one goes
Introduces a conditional situation: if one goes to another park…
Verb stem + すぎる indicates excess; 伸びすぎて means having grown too tall or long.
Links causes and results: overgrown grass → the ball stops → playing becomes impossible. The omitted activity with できません is understood from context.
So I go to places such as somewhat wider roads.
Marks examples: 道路など means roads and similar places.
However, on concrete, I cannot play freely because I am afraid of falling.
で marks the setting or surface, and は highlights it: on concrete…
Plain-form verb + 場合 indicates a situation; 転ぶ場合 refers to a situation in which one falls.
恐れて gives the reason for the following negative statement: being afraid, one cannot…
遊べません is the polite negative potential form of 遊ぶ: cannot play.
As a result, my friends could no longer play sports and became bored, and they gradually went outside to play less often.
Expresses a change to a negative state: できなくなる means to become unable to do something.
An い-adjective stem + くなる expresses a change of state; つまらなくなり means becoming bored, with なり connecting clauses.
Indicates small increments: 少しずつ means little by little.
Here it emphasizes a completed, regrettable result: the children ended up playing outside less often.
Because I would rather exercise outside than stay at home, I do long-distance running, which only requires a road.
Marks the comparison: preferring outdoor exercise to staying at home.
Gives a desire as the reason: because one wants to…
Expresses a minimum sufficient condition: 道さえあれば means as long as there is a road.
Here it describes a regular activity: taking up long-distance running as a habit.
But doing nothing but long-distance running gets boring (note 3).
Frames a situation limited to one thing: with only long-distance running…; it implies this is insufficient to sustain interest.
So I want parks and an environment for playing sports to be secured, with safety taken into account.
Verb stem + ながら indicates simultaneous actions; here it means taking safety into account while securing places for sports.
Expresses a wish for someone else to do something: to secure parks and an environment for sports. The responsible person is unspecified.
Lists representative items: parks and a suitable environment.
Question 2: directly states the boy's wish, matching option 2: an environment for sports, without limiting it to one sport.
Question 3: the proposal identifies an environment for sports that takes safety into account as important, matching option 2.
If that happens, wouldn't many children be more inclined to go outside and play?
do; show an intention in ～ようとする
Expresses a condition: そうなれば refers to securing the parks and sports environment described in the previous sentence.
Volitional verb + とする expresses an intention or attempt; here it suggests becoming inclined to play outside.
Softly offers an opinion or prediction and invites agreement: wouldn't…?
Question 3: そう refers to securing the environment in the previous sentence; a suitable environment would encourage children to play outside, supporting option 2.
(Note 1) Playing catch: a sport used for baseball practice.
States the purpose of the following noun: a sport for baseball practice.
Explains what a term refers to: here 芝 refers to grass.
(Note 3) Get bored: come to dislike something or become fed up with it.
With a な-adjective, the adjective stem + になる expresses a change of state: いやになる means to become fed up with something.
Children spend less time playing sports outdoors because fewer places are available for exercise. This concerns usable places, not necessarily the number of parks.
Parks have prohibition signs or overgrown grass, while concrete roads make the boy afraid of falling and prevent unrestricted play.
Being unable to play sports leaves the boy's friends bored, so they gradually play outside less often.
The boy chooses long-distance running because it only requires a road, but doing just one sport becomes boring.
A wish for a suitable sports environment
The boy wants parks and an environment for sports to be secured with safety in mind. He believes this would encourage more children to play outside, highlighting the importance of the environment.
Defines playing catch, lawn grass, and becoming bored.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t16-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, I think children have been spending less time playing sports outdoors. I think one reason that can be given is that there are fewer places where children can exercise.

When I go to a park wanting to play soccer, there is a sign saying that soccer and playing catch (note 1) are prohibited. When I go to another park, the grass (note 2) has grown too tall, stopping the ball and making it impossible to play. So I go to places such as somewhat wider roads. However, on concrete, I cannot play freely because I am afraid of falling.

As a result, my friends could no longer play sports and became bored, and they gradually went outside to play less often.

Because I would rather exercise outside than stay at home, I do long-distance running, which only requires a road. But doing nothing but long-distance running gets boring (note 3). So I want parks and an environment for playing sports to be secured, with safety taken into account. If that happens, wouldn't many children be more inclined to go outside and play?

(Note 1) Playing catch: a sport used for baseball practice.

(Note 2) 芝: grass.

(Note 3) Get bored: come to dislike something or become fed up with it.
Being impatient and prone to rushing, I make it a rule every year to begin my major cleaning as soon as New Year postcards go on sale (November 25).
で connects a な-adjective to what follows: impatient and prone to rushing.
At the same time as; as soon as another event occurs.
Make it a rule to do something and maintain that practice.
That season has come around again this year.
Expresses a change of state or the arrival of a time; here, that season has arrived.
First, I organize the letters I received over the past year, utility payment receipts, and similar papers, then put them in a large envelope for safekeeping.
The preceding clause modifies the noun: letters received during that period. いただく is the humble form of もらう.
Lists examples without making an exhaustive list.
Connects actions in sequence: organize, put away, and store.
Next comes organizing and tidying the drawers of the chest of drawers and the cupboard.
や lists items; here, 引き出し refers to the drawers of the listed types of furniture.
A noun-ending sentence omits a verb such as する; the action of organizing is implied.
Evidence for Question 2: the small places cleaned first are drawers, so the answer is option 2, 引き出し.
My husband tells me, “Get rid of anything you do not use for a year.”
Be told or instructed to do something. Here, ように is inside the quotation.
A negative verb modifies もの: things that one does not do something with.
Evidence for Question 3: this states the required practice of discarding items unused for a year; the next sentence shows the writer does not follow it.
However, someone who grew up in a time of scarcity, as I did, feels reluctant to do so and often puts away again the things they had intended to throw out.
の replaces が in a noun-modifying clause: a period when material goods were scarce.
Marks the person experiencing the feeling: for someone who grew up in those circumstances.
Intended or attempted to do something; here, intended to throw something away.
Evidence for Question 1: growing up with scarcity explains the feeling that discarding things would be wasteful.
Question 1: putting things away again shows a feeling of wastefulness, so option 3, もったいない, is correct. Question 3: this shows failure to discard items unused for a year, so option 2 is correct.
The major cleaning, which began with small areas, progresses day by day to the living room, the Japanese-style room, and the bedroom.
A noun-modifying clause: the major cleaning that began with small areas.
Progress or move on toward the next place or stage.
Evidence for Question 2: this refers back to the drawers as the starting places.
These rooms are cleaned later, ruling out 居間 and 和室 for Question 2.
Among these areas, the kitchen is particularly difficult to clean.
A nominal predicate omits final だ: the difficult area is the kitchen.
The simmered dishes and lighting fixtures are in the worst condition.
Describes the condition of something; final だ is omitted here.
At times like this, my husband is the one I can rely on; he uses kerosene to polish things for me in a sunny spot in the garden.
Nominalizes the preceding clause to identify someone: the dependable person is the husband; で connects to the next clause.
の replaces が in a noun-modifying clause: a garden area with good sunlight.
Use something as a means of performing an action.
Someone does something for the speaker, often conveying gratitude.
The secret to major cleaning is everyday care and keeping things organized and tidy.
から combines with の to modify a noun: care maintained from ordinary daily life onward.
Identifies two elements of the secret: everyday care and tidiness.
Frames Question 3: compare this principle with keeping items meant for disposal in sentences 4–5 to select option 2.
I think this may be precisely the secret to finishing the cleaning cheerfully.
Expresses an opinion tentatively: I think this may well be…
(Note 1) Impatient: being unable to take one's time or remain calm.
A negative expression modifies 様子, describing a state in which an action or quality is absent.
(Note 2) Day by day: each successive day.
(Note 3) Knack: a good way of doing something.
A time expression modifies a noun: a good method for when one does something.
The writer introduces her impatient nature and her rule of starting major cleaning when New Year postcards go on sale.
Organizing possessions and reluctance to discard

The writer stores papers and tidies drawers. Although her husband tells her to discard items unused for a year, she often keeps them because she grew up with scarcity. This provides the main evidence for all three questions.
Moving through the rooms with her husband's help
Cleaning progresses from small areas to whole rooms. The kitchen is difficult, and the husband helps polish things in the garden.
The secret lies in everyday habits
The writer concludes that everyday care and tidiness make major cleaning enjoyable; compare this with her failure to discard unused items to answer Question 3.
Explains three expressions: impatient, day by day, and knack.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t18-p1.vietnamese:
Being impatient and prone to rushing, I make it a rule every year to begin my major cleaning as soon as New Year postcards go on sale (November 25). That season has come around again this year.

First, I organize the letters I received over the past year, utility payment receipts, and similar papers, then put them in a large envelope for safekeeping. Next comes organizing and tidying the drawers of the chest of drawers and the cupboard. My husband tells me, “Get rid of anything you do not use for a year.” However, someone who grew up in a time of scarcity, as I did, feels reluctant to do so and often puts away again the things they had intended to throw out.

The major cleaning, which began with small areas, progresses day by day to the living room, the Japanese-style room, and the bedroom. Among these areas, the kitchen is particularly difficult to clean. The simmered dishes and lighting fixtures are in the worst condition. At times like this, my husband is the one I can rely on; he uses kerosene to polish things for me in a sunny spot in the garden.

The secret to major cleaning is everyday care and keeping things organized and tidy. I think this may be precisely the secret to finishing the cleaning cheerfully.

(Note 1) Impatient: being unable to take one's time or remain calm.

(Note 2) Day by day: each successive day.

(Note 3) Knack: a good way of doing something.
The festival season, filled with the resounding beat of drums, has come again this year.
In 今年も, も indicates that the festival season has come this year too.
太鼓の音が鳴り響く modifies お祭り: a festival where drums resound.
There are many Shinto shrines in the town where we live, and at each shrine, people carry flower floats and portable shrines in slow processions through the neighborhood.
States that something exists in a place; には marks the location as the topic.
After a noun, means “each” or “every”; 神社ごとに means “at each shrine.”
Lists examples without necessarily giving an exhaustive list.
担いで connects carrying the floats and shrines with walking in procession.
を marks the area traversed; 町内を練り歩く means to parade through the neighborhood.
We moved to this town when my twin daughters, now eight, were about to turn three.
Expresses a change; 3歳になる means to turn three.
Indicates an approximate time; 3歳になる頃 means around the time of turning three.
In 引っ越してきた, indicates moving toward the location used as the narrator’s viewpoint.
At the festivals, everyone from young children to older people comes together and joins in the excitement.
Sets the context being discussed: at the festivals.
Expresses an inclusive range: from young children to older people.
一体になって describes people coming together as one and sharing the excitement.
My daughters, who had never even held a drumstick before, have now improved to the point where they can play the drums.
Gives an example with emphasis: they had never even held something like a drumstick.
Had never even done something; も emphasizes the complete lack of prior experience.
今では means “now,” contrasting the present with the past.
Expresses a change in ability; 叩けるようになる means to become able to play the drums.
Marks the extent reached: improving to the point of being able to play the drums.
Evidence for Question 1, option 3: the girls can now play the drums; 太鼓 supplies the understood object of 叩ける.
Through festivals and similar occasions, my two daughters learn manners and what the town used to be like from local people, learning something new every day.
To learn from someone; から marks the person providing the instruction.
Through an activity or occasion; here, through festivals.
Gives representative examples, implying that there are others.
Lists examples of what the girls learn, including manners and the town’s past.
In 日々学んでいる, expresses regular, ongoing learning.
Evidence for Question 2: the environment is the town with festivals, where the girls interact with and learn from local people.
Direct evidence for Question 3, option 3: the children grow by learning new things every day.
Although nuclear families have become common today, I feel grateful for this environment, where my children can grow while learning many things through these interactions.
“Has become…, but…”; contrasts the prevalence of nuclear families with the children’s community interactions.
Indicates the means of learning: through those interactions.
Attaches to a verb’s ます stem to express concurrent activities: growing while learning.
成長できる is the potential form of 成長する, meaning “can grow and develop.”
Expresses how something is perceived; この環境をありがたく感じる means to feel grateful for this environment.
Question 2 takes option 1: “this environment” is the town with festivals, where the girls interact, learn, and grow, as described in the preceding sentence.
Supports Question 3, option 3: growth is linked to learning many things, matching the daily learning described previously.
(Note 1) 練り歩く: to form a procession and walk slowly.
Connects forming a procession with walking slowly.
(Note 2) バチ: a wooden stick used to play a drum.
Indicates when an action occurs: when playing a drum.
The preceding clause modifies the noun: a wooden stick used when playing a drum.
Introduces the festival season through the sound of drums and describes shrine processions around town.
The daughters learn to play drums
The family moved here when the twins were about three. Amid festivals that bring all ages together, the girls progressed from never holding drumsticks to being able to play.
Through festivals and interactions with local people, the girls learn new things daily. The narrator appreciates the town environment that helps them learn and grow.
Defines 練り歩く as walking slowly in procession and バチ as a wooden drumstick.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t19-p1.vietnamese:
The festival season, filled with the resounding beat of drums, has come again this year. There are many Shinto shrines in the town where we live, and at each shrine, people carry flower floats and portable shrines in slow processions through the neighborhood.

We moved to this town when my twin daughters, now eight, were about to turn three. At the festivals, everyone from young children to older people comes together and joins in the excitement. My daughters, who had never even held a drumstick before, have now improved to the point where they can play the drums.

Through festivals and similar occasions, my two daughters learn manners and what the town used to be like from local people, learning something new every day. Although nuclear families have become common today, I feel grateful for this environment, where my children can grow while learning many things through these interactions.

(Note 1) 練り歩く: to form a procession and walk slowly.

(Note 2) バチ: a wooden stick used to play a drum.
Mika, a fourth grader, has lived with a prosthetic leg since she began walking.
Added to a verb stem to indicate the start of an action; 歩き出す means to begin walking.
Since around the time when…; marks the beginning of an ongoing situation.
で marks the means or circumstances of living, here living with a prosthetic leg.
Describes a continuing situation: she lives with a prosthetic leg.
Evidence for Question 3: she has used a prosthetic leg since she began walking, supporting option 1, a person with a disability.
This happened at Kugino Elementary School, a small school at the foot of Mount Aso with just one class per grade.
Introduces a name: the school called Kugino Elementary School.
Indicates location; 阿蘇山の麓にある modifies 学校.
で marks where something happens, and の connects it to a noun: an incident at the school.
In May this year, when she wore shorts to practice for sports day, first graders who saw the prosthetic leg attached below her knee for the first time called it a “fake leg.”
When an action has occurred or a situation holds: when she wore shorts.
A modifying clause precedes its noun: 膝下に付けた modifies 義足, and 義足を初めて見た modifies 1年生.
Passive expression meaning someone said something to the subject; から identifies the speaker and と marks the quoted words.
Evidence for Question 2: being told she had a “fake leg” was hurtful, matching option 3, having her prosthetic leg mocked. This does not establish deliberate malice.

Encouraged by her homeroom teacher, who said, “They simply don't know about prosthetic legs; they probably mean no harm,” she ①gathered her courage and spoke openly about her situation in the first graders’ classroom.
Here, だけ limits the explanation to simply not knowing, and で links it to the next statement. It does not mean that merely doing something is sufficient.
Expresses an expectation based on reasoning: they presumably mean no harm.
Passive of 勧める: to be advised or encouraged by someone. 勧められ links this to the following action.
Links actions or describes how an action is performed: gathering courage and speaking.
Evidence for Question 1: the courage was to speak openly about her prosthetic leg to the first graders, so option 3 is correct.
Understanding spread, and Mika overcame ②the emotional shock.
A verb's masu-stem links clauses in written language; 広がり functions like 広がって.
For Question 2, “the shock” refers back to the “fake leg” remark in sentence index 2; the cause must be identified from that earlier sentence.
Now the first graders reassure her, saying, “We'll explain it to the children who start school next year, so don't worry.”
all right, nothing to worry about
A clause modifies the following noun: 来年入学する子 means children who will enter school next year.
Gives a reason: she need not worry because they will explain.
Marks an action benefiting the speaker or viewpoint character; here, the children's words reassure Mika.
“I was able to express my feelings, and I felt more at ease.
Expresses ability. でき is the linking form of できる, connecting the ability to speak with the resulting relief.
Means to become; nouns and na-adjectives take に. 楽になった means to have become more at ease.
I'd be happy if people struggling in the same way could feel, ‘I'll take the plunge and try speaking up,’” Mika says with a smile.
Indicates manner or similarity: 同じように悩む means to struggle in the same way.
Volitional form of ～てみる: let's try, or I'll try doing something.
Come to have the feeling or intention expressed in the preceding quotation.

Expresses happiness if someone does or experiences something hoped for. The original 人が…なってもらえれば is somewhat irregular; the usual construction is 人に…なってもらえれば. The intended meaning is that she hopes others will also feel ready to speak up.
A reporting construction with an omitted final verb; にっこり depicts Mika smiling as she speaks.
Her dream is to become a writer.
The sentence ends with a noun and omits だ; it means that her dream is to be a writer.
She writes compositions about everyday events and will join the basketball club in September.
belong to, be a member of
書き is the masu-stem of 書く, used to link two activities in written language.
から marks a starting point, while は highlights the period from September onward.
Means to belong to an organization or club; に marks the organization.
Her goal is to compete in the Paralympic Games.
Identifies a goal: competing in the Paralympic Games.
Supporting evidence for Question 3: her Paralympic goal is consistent with her being a person with a disability; the direct evidence remains her prosthetic leg in sentence 0.
Introduces Mika, a fourth grader who has used a prosthetic leg since early childhood, and her small school at the foot of Mount Aso.
Hurt and the courage to speak
The “fake leg” remark shocks Mika. Encouraged by her teacher, she explains her situation honestly to the first graders, increasing understanding and overcoming the hurt.
The first graders promise to explain things to new pupils. Mika feels relieved after expressing herself and hopes others in similar situations will also find the courage to speak.
Mika wants to become a writer, writes about everyday events, will join the basketball club in September, and aims to compete in the Paralympic Games.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t20-p1.vietnamese:
Mika, a fourth grader, has lived with a prosthetic leg since she began walking. This happened at Kugino Elementary School, a small school at the foot of Mount Aso with just one class per grade.

In May this year, when she wore shorts to practice for sports day, first graders who saw the prosthetic leg attached below her knee for the first time called it a “fake leg.” Encouraged by her homeroom teacher, who said, “They simply don't know about prosthetic legs; they probably mean no harm,” she gathered her courage and spoke openly about her situation in the first graders’ classroom. Understanding spread, and Mika overcame the emotional shock.

Now the first graders reassure her, saying, “We'll explain it to the children who start school next year, so don't worry.” With a smile, Mika says, “I was able to express my feelings, and I felt more at ease. I'd be happy if people struggling in the same way could feel, ‘I'll take the plunge and try speaking up.’”

Her dream is to become a writer. She writes compositions about everyday events and will join the basketball club in September. Her goal is to compete in the Paralympic Games.
At the end of last year, I decided to stop using email on my mobile phone.
Decide to do something; やめることにした means decided to stop.
Starting about seven years ago, some time after email became available on mobile phones, I was drawn to its convenience and often enjoyed sending emails to friends and acquaintances.
Expresses a change in ability or state: email became usable on mobile phones.
Turns an adjective into a noun expressing a quality: 便利 → 便利さ, convenience.
Be attracted to something; here, its convenience.
Expresses repetition: repeatedly sending emails and enjoying it.
Describes an ongoing state or habitual action in the past.
Question 1: explicitly identifies convenience as the initial attraction, supporting option 4.
However, from around the time last summer had passed, I noticed that the more I used it, the lonelier I became.
The more…, the more…; 利用すればするだけ links greater use to a greater effect.
Become…; an い-adjective changes to its ～く form before なる.
Expresses a continuing change: loneliness progressively increases.
Notice something. 心が寂しくなっていく modifies 自分: the writer notices their own increasing loneliness.
In my case, because emails were easy to compose using just my fingers, I often composed mobile emails while doing something else, such as housework.
In the case of…; 私の場合 limits the statement to the writer's experience.
With only…; here, using just one's fingers, not necessarily a single finger.
Gives a reason: because composing emails is easy and convenient.
Do one action while doing another; attaches to the verb's ます stem.
Often do…; 作成していることが多かった describes a frequent situation in the past.
As a result, emails made up of short sentences caused misunderstandings between me and the recipient, sometimes leaving me with an uneasy sense of danger.
Marks a cause: misunderstandings arose because of emails made up of short sentences.
Between oneself and…; here, between the writer and the recipient.
Expresses an unintended or regrettable result.
There were also times when…; describes an occasional situation in the past.
Question 3: emails consisting of short sentences cause misunderstandings, matching option 3.
After that, over the period from the end of the year into the new year, I keep in touch with friends and acquaintances for about two weeks.
From… through around…; marks an approximate time span. にかけ is a connective form of にかけて.
Modifies a noun with the meaning with…: 友人、知人とのやりとり means exchanges with friends and acquaintances.
Through postcards and phone calls, I enjoy communicating through written words and voices.
Lists examples without necessarily giving an exhaustive list.
Marks a means: by postcard or telephone.
Modifies a noun to indicate a medium: communication through written words and voices.
Expresses an ongoing activity or current state.
Question 2: identifies the communication referred to by そこ in the next sentence, clarifying the contrast with email.
That way of communicating brings great joy and warmth that I did not feel when exchanging emails while doing something else.
Modifies a noun: email exchanges carried out while doing something else.
Expresses a contrasting negative: those email exchanges did not provide that feeling.
A past-form clause modifies a noun; 感じなかった modifies 大きな喜びと温かさ despite the intervening comma.
Forms a noun from an adjective: 温かい → 温かさ, emotional warmth.
Question 2: the contrast shows that email did not give the writer a feeling of warmth, supporting option 1. This describes the writer's experience, not all email.
Note: 手軽さ means the quality of being easy to do and convenient.
Easy to do…; attaches to the verb's ます stem. やりやすく is the connective form linking it to 便利な.
The writer opens with the decision to stop using mobile email, then recalls its initial appeal of convenience and the loneliness that later grew.
Because emails were easy to compose, the writer often wrote them while doing other things. Emails consisting of short sentences led to misunderstandings with recipients.
Contact through postcards and calls around the New Year brings joy and warmth. This contrast explains the loneliness the writer felt when using email.
Defines 手軽さ as the quality of being easy to do and convenient.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t21-p1.vietnamese:
At the end of last year, I decided to stop using email on my mobile phone. Starting about seven years ago, some time after email became available on mobile phones, I was drawn to its convenience and often enjoyed sending emails to friends and acquaintances. However, from around the time last summer had passed, I noticed that the more I used it, the lonelier I became.

In my case, because emails were easy to compose using just my fingers, I often composed mobile emails while doing something else, such as housework. As a result, emails made up of short sentences caused misunderstandings between me and the recipient, sometimes leaving me with an uneasy sense of danger.

After that, over the period from the end of the year into the new year, I keep in touch with friends and acquaintances for about two weeks. Through postcards and phone calls, I enjoy communicating through written words and voices. That way of communicating brings great joy and warmth that I did not feel when exchanging emails while doing something else.

Note: 手軽さ means the quality of being easy to do and convenient.
Among public services, I think libraries are particularly wonderful.
Among…, especially…; singles out one member of a group.
Expresses an opinion the speaker holds.
You can borrow books, CDs, and DVDs for free, and the library also screens films.
Lists representative examples without making the list exhaustive.
The potential form of a group-two verb; 借りられます here means “can borrow.”
Adds another advantage or reason: and also…
There is an impressive municipal library near my home, so during the summer vacation too, I went there with my mother about four or five times a week to read books, do homework, and so on.
used to do, among other activities
Gives the reason the narrator regularly visited the library.
Expresses approximate frequency: about four or five times a week here.
Lists representative activities, such as reading and doing homework.
Here, describes a repeated habit in the past.
My mother said, “Perhaps because of the economic downturn, there are more users than in a typical year.”
cause, usually with a negative connotation
Perhaps because of…; suggests a possible cause without certainty.
Makes a comparison: more numerous than in a typical year.
A sentence ending expressing a reaction and seeking agreement, often associated with feminine speech.
Question 2: the specific social situation mentioned is the economic downturn, which 世の中の様子 later refers back to. Choose option 1.
Although it is a library I am so fond of, during the five-day holiday in September it was closed for three consecutive days, from the 21st to the 23rd.
Although…; shifts from praise to a point of dissatisfaction.
In 21～23日と3日間, と connects the stated dates with their duration: the 21st through the 23rd, totaling three days.
Describes the library's closed state during a past period.
Question 1: establishes a five-day holiday with closure on the 21st–23rd. Together with visits on the 19th and 20th, this identifies the holiday as the 19th–23rd.
This was because the 21st was a Monday, the library's regular closing day, and the 22nd and 23rd were public holidays.
で is the connective form of だ after a noun: the 21st was Monday and a regular closing day.
This is because…; explains the reason for the preceding statement.
Question 1: clarifies the schedule for the final three days, the 21st–23rd: a regular closing day followed by two public holidays.
I too went on the 19th and 20th, and then had no choice but to read the books I had borrowed at home.
Connects actions in sequence: visiting the library and then reading at home.
Here, indicates borrowing books and bringing them back.
Verb dictionary form + しかない means “have no choice but to…”; used here in the polite past form.
Question 1: the visits were on the 19th and 20th. Combined with closure on the 21st–23rd, the five-day holiday runs from the 19th through the 23rd. Choose option 2.
Surely many residents, myself included, wanted to use the library during the holiday, didn't they?
Including… as well; the narrator includes themself among residents with this wish.
Expresses a wish held in the past.
Softens a conjecture or opinion while inviting agreement.
Question 3: identifies residents' desire to use the library during the holiday, supporting the final request to keep it open.

The people who work at the library presumably have their own circumstances, but I felt it was also necessary to serve residents by adapting to social conditions and their wishes—for example, shifting closing days to less busy weekdays so the library could open during the holiday.
Presumably… but…; acknowledges the staff's circumstances before presenting an opinion.
Adapt to…; here, social conditions and residents' wishes.
の can replace が in a noun-modifying clause: 利用者の少ない平日 means weekdays with fewer users.
By doing things such as…; presents rescheduling closing days as an example.
し in 開館し is the connective stem of 開館する, linking opening the library with serving residents.
I thought it might also be necessary to…; こと nominalizes the action, and the expression makes a tentative suggestion. It does not mean “unnecessary.”
Question 2: this phrase refers to the social situation introduced in sentence 3 (zero-based), namely 不況, the economic downturn. Choose option 1.
Question 3: the narrator proposes moving closing days to less busy weekdays so the library can open during the consecutive holidays. Choose option 4.
The narrator values the library's free services and visits regularly with their mother. The mother's reference to the economic downturn explains what 世の中の様子 refers to.
The library was closed on the 21st–23rd for its regular closing day and public holidays. The narrator visited on the 19th and 20th; together, these dates establish the five-day holiday as the 19th–23rd.
Request to open during the holiday
The narrator believes many residents wanted to use the library during the holiday and proposes shifting closing days to quieter weekdays to accommodate social conditions and residents' needs.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t22-p1.vietnamese:
Among public services, I think libraries are particularly wonderful. You can borrow books, CDs, and DVDs for free, and the library also screens films. There is an impressive municipal library near my home, so during the summer vacation too, I went there with my mother about four or five times a week to read books, do homework, and so on. My mother said, “Perhaps because of the economic downturn, there are more users than in a typical year.”

Although it is a library I am so fond of, during the five-day holiday in September it was closed for three consecutive days, from the 21st to the 23rd. This was because the 21st was a Monday, the library's regular closing day, and the 22nd and 23rd were public holidays. I too went on the 19th and 20th, and then had no choice but to read the books I had borrowed at home. Surely many residents, myself included, wanted to use the library during the holiday, didn't they?

The people who work at the library presumably have their own circumstances, but I felt it was also necessary to serve residents by adapting to social conditions and their wishes—for example, shifting closing days to less busy weekdays so the library could open during the holiday.
Shortly after I was born, my father collapsed from an illness, leaving behind me at six months old and my four-year-old brother, and departed for heaven.
Expresses completion of an action or an unfortunate, irreversible event with sorrow or regret.
Shortly after doing something / shortly after an event occurs.

The father passed away and departed for heaven ('天国へ旅立ってしまいました') when the author was six months old. Therefore, when she asks '②見てて、お父さん' (Watch over me, Dad), the father is watching from heaven (Option 1 is correct for Question 2).
Since then, my mother has worked tirelessly and raised the two of us.
Someone does an action beneficial to the speaker/speaker's family with gratitude.
Not knowing my father's face and having no memory of him playing with me, I must have felt lonely when I was little.
Formal written negative form of a verb (= ～ないで), connecting clauses.
Receive a favor/action done by someone.
Must be / should be (confident conjecture based on reasons).
However, my grandparents' family lived nearby, so I grew up being warmly loved and cherished.
Passive voice: かわいがられる (to be loved/doted upon).
To grow up in a certain manner or state.

During winter vacation, when I was organizing photo albums, while my brother had plenty of photos playing happily with our father, I only had a single photo of being held by my father in front of the Hinamatsuri dolls.
there was nothing but / only had
When doing an action, discovering or noticing a contrasting fact.
Only / nothing but (used with negative verb to emphasize scarcity).

The author was sulking/grumbling (ごねてる) because while her older brother had lots of photos playing happily with their father, she had only one photo (Option 3 is correct: there are many photos of father with brother, but few with the author). Option 1 is incorrect because she did have one photo; Option 2 is incorrect because the father did hold her; Option 4 was not the complaint she made when viewing the album.
Seeing me pouting, my grandmother told me stories about my father.
When/while doing something, discovering the subsequent development or action.
Someone kindly does an action for me.

That my father, a pharmacist, was kind and trusted by sick people; that when I came home from the maternity clinic, he held me with immense joy and would not let me go; and that when he was hospitalized due to illness, he left a message on the computer for my brother and me promising that he would definitely return by the Hinamatsuri festival.
Nominalizing multiple clauses with こと to list the points grandmother recounted.
Deadline marker: by (a specified time or event).

The detail that moved the author's heart deeply (胸が熱くなりました) in the stories told was that when hospitalized, the father left a message on the computer promising to return by Hinamatsuri (Option 4 is correct: the father left a certain message). Options 1 and 3 are merely background details; Option 2 was mentioned at the beginning of the text.
My heart warmed and swelled with deep emotion.
Idiom: to be deeply touched, heart stirred with warm/intense emotion.
The phrase '胸が熱くなりました' indicates the profound emotional impact left on the author after learning about her father's love and message (reinforces the evidence for Question 3).
In the spring, I will become a junior high school student.
Change of state or role: to become something.
Once I enter junior high, I will do my absolute best toward my dreams, so please watch over me, Dad.
watch over (me) (short for 見ていて)
Toward / aiming for a goal or direction.
Contraction of ～ていて, expressing a continuous affectionate plea or request.

The author lovingly appeals to her late father to watch over her from heaven (where he departed to according to the opening sentence: '天国へ旅立ってしまいました'). Thus the father watches from heaven (Option 1 is correct for Question 2).
(Note 1) ごねる: to complain, grumble, or pout
(Note 2) ひなまつり (Hinamatsuri): an event held on March 3rd for girls
For the sake of / for the benefit of someone.
The father fell ill and departed for heaven when the author was only six months old; the mother worked tirelessly to raise the two children.
Childhood without father and pouting over the photo album
Despite growing up warmly with grandparents nearby, the author felt upset upon discovering her brother had many photos with their father while she only had one.
Grandmother's story of father's profound love
Grandmother recounted how overjoyed the father was holding the newborn author and the touching promise he left on the computer before being hospitalized, deeply moving the author.
Promise for the future addressed to father in heaven
About to enter junior high school, the author resolves to work hard toward dreams and asks her father in heaven to watch over her; followed by vocabulary notes.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t23-p1.vietnamese:
Shortly after I was born, my father collapsed from an illness, leaving behind me at six months old and my four-year-old brother, and departed for heaven. Since then, my mother has worked tirelessly to raise the two of us.

Having never seen my father's face and having no memories of him playing with me, I must have felt lonely when I was young. However, my grandparents' family lived nearby, so I grew up surrounded by their warm love and affection. During winter vacation, while sorting through the photo albums, I noticed that my brother had plenty of photos playing happily with our father, whereas I had only a single photo of being held by my father in front of the Hinamatsuri dolls.

Seeing me pout, my grandmother told me stories about my father: how he was a gentle pharmacist trusted by patients, how he held me with immense joy and refused to let go when I came home from the maternity clinic, and how, upon being hospitalized for illness, he left a message on the computer for my brother and me promising that he would definitely return by Hinamatsuri. My heart warmed with deep emotion.

This spring, I will enter junior high school. Once I enter junior high, I will do my absolute best toward my dreams, so please watch over me, Dad.

(Note 1) ごねる: to grumble, complain, or pout
(Note 2) ひなまつり: a festival held on March 3rd for girls
I used to play rugby in my school club.
Marks the setting of an activity: in a school club.
Describes an ongoing or habitual activity in the past.
Throughout that time, my mother was my greatest source of support.
Identifies the highest degree or most prominent member within a scope.
Emphasizes identity: the person providing the greatest support was the mother.
Question 3: establishes that the mother supported the writer.
My mother is a civil servant rather than a full-time homemaker. She works hard from morning until evening every day, sometimes even past 9 p.m.
Means 'not … but …'; で links this to the following information.
Marks a time span from … to ….
Means 'there are also days when …,' indicating occasional occurrence.
Question 3: the mother is a civil servant, ruling out both full-time homemaker options.
