Despite how much she works, what always puzzles me is that she never shows me a tired expression when she comes home.
Attaches to a verb stem; here it has a concessive sense: despite working so much.
Nominalizes both clauses to specify what puzzles the writer: the mother not showing fatigue.
Marks the time when an action has occurred: when the mother has arrived home.
Question 3: she does not show fatigue, contradicting option 2.
Seeing her like that, I feel that she is incredibly strong as an individual, apart from her role as a mother.
Means 'not in the capacity of … but as …'; shifts the perspective from motherhood to individual character.
Means 'feel that …'; んだ adds a sense of realization, and と marks the content of the feeling.
Every morning, my mother gets up around five and makes a packed lunch for me.
Uses a verb stem to connect actions, equivalent here to 起きて.
Someone does something for the speaker's benefit; here, the mother makes the writer lunch.
Question 3: making lunch every day is a concrete example of the mother's care and support.
My mother's cooking is so delicious that you could call it the best in the world.
Means 'so … that one could say …,' emphasizing a very high degree.
Question 1: the writer genuinely loves the cooking, so the criticism is not caused by bad food.
Yet I have been doing something that wrongs such a caring mother.
Means to do something one feels sorry toward someone for; に marks that person.
Describes an ongoing or repeated action or behavior.

When eating my lunch at school, I would put on a tough act, saying things like, “Today's side dishes are the worst” and “This makes me lose my appetite,” and tell the friends around me that my mother's packed lunches tasted awful.
Marks when an action takes place: while eating lunch at school.
A Kansai dialect ending; や corresponds to だ, while わ adds an expressive tone.
Means to lose the desire to do something; here, to lose the desire to eat.
Introduces examples of what someone says: saying things like ….
と marks the claim being spread; ～ていた describes repeated behavior in the past.
Question 1: the writer puts on an act before friends. Combined with the sincere praise and subsequent denial, this implies embarrassment about praising the lunch; choose 1.
Question 2: directly identifies the action being apologized for: telling everyone the mother's lunch tasted bad; choose 3.
But in truth, I have never once thought that.
do not think; have not thought
は contrasts the writer's true feelings with what was said to friends.
Means 'not even once,' completely negating an experience or action.
Question 1: 'that' refers to thinking the lunch tasted bad; the denial shows the criticism was an act. Question 2: it clarifies that the writer said something contrary to their true feelings.
I would like to take this opportunity to apologize to my mother.
An idiomatic expression meaning to take this opportunity to say something.
Means 'want to apologize to someone'; に marks the recipient and ～たい expresses desire.
“I'm sorry, Mom. Your packed lunches are always absolutely delicious”…
Mom; an affectionate form of address
で connects the noun predicate 絶品 with the adjective おいしい: superb and delicious.
A sentence-final particle emphasizing what the speaker wants to convey, here a sincere assurance to the mother.
と marks the quotation; the following verb is omitted, linking back to the desire to apologize in the previous sentence.
Question 1: confirms that the writer has always found the lunch delicious, reinforcing that the criticism was an act. Question 2: the apology corrects the negative claim previously spread.
(Note 1) 部活: activities of a student group or club.
Used in a definition to mean 'refers to …'.
(Note 2) Rugby: a type of football played with fifteen people on each team.
Means 'a type of …'; で connects it to the next description.
Means to play with the stated number of people; で marks the participant count.
Means 'one of …'; here, one of the sports.
The writer introduces their school rugby experience and identifies their mother as their greatest source of support.
The mother is a civil servant who works long hours without showing her child a tired expression. This puzzles the writer and makes them see her strength as an individual.
The mother gets up early to make lunch every day. The claim that her cooking is the best in the world reveals the writer's sincere opinion.
Putting on an act before friends

The writer admits to telling friends the lunch tasted bad despite never thinking so. The contrast between outward criticism and true feelings implies embarrassment about praising it before friends; spreading that claim is also the act requiring an apology.
The writer takes this opportunity to apologize and sincerely tell their mother that her lunches are always delicious, correcting the earlier criticism.
The two notes explain the club activities and rugby mentioned at the beginning.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t24-p1.vietnamese:
I used to play rugby in my school club. Throughout that time, my mother was my greatest source of support.

My mother is a civil servant rather than a full-time homemaker. She works hard from morning until evening every day, sometimes even past 9 p.m. Despite how much she works, what always puzzles me is that she never shows me a tired expression when she comes home. Seeing her like that, I feel that she is incredibly strong as an individual, apart from her role as a mother.

Every morning, my mother gets up around five and makes a packed lunch for me. Her cooking is so delicious that you could call it the best in the world. Yet I have been doing something that wrongs such a caring mother. When eating my lunch at school, I would put on a tough act, saying things like, “Today's side dishes are the worst” and “This makes me lose my appetite,” and tell the friends around me that my mother's packed lunches tasted awful. But in truth, I have never once thought that. I would like to take this opportunity to apologize to my mother. “I'm sorry, Mom. Your packed lunches are always absolutely delicious”…

(Note 1) 部活: activities of a student group or club.

(Note 2) Rugby: a type of football played with fifteen people on each team.
The other day, a piano concert admitting children from age zero was held at a hall in the ward.
Marks a starting point, here the minimum age for admission.
Expresses ability or permission; 入場できる means admission is allowed.
States that an event took place.
The performance was wonderful, but I was disappointed by some people's poor manners.
Introduces background followed by a contrast: a good performance but poor manners.
Forms a noun from an adjective stem: 悪い → 悪さ.
Expresses disappointment with something; は highlights its target.
Even during the performance, people kept going in and out of the hall, and children's voices rang out again and again.
Attaches to an activity noun to mean during that activity.
Means even though, expressing dissatisfaction with an unexpected situation.
Lists representative actions or events. The final する is omitted here.
Q1: Specifies the poor manners. Repeated noise from children supports option 3: some parents let their children be noisy.
It was so bad that a man seated toward the front turned around between pieces twice to say, “Please be quiet.” I really felt sorry for the pianist.
After a quantity, emphasizes how much or how many: 2度も means as many as twice.
静かにする means to keep quiet or refrain from making noise.
Uses と to quote the content of an admonition.
Means to such an extent that; the two admonitions illustrate how disruptive the noise was.
Q1: The request shows that the noise disturbed listeners. The admonition was a response to poor manners, not the behavior being criticized.
Q1: The writer felt sorry for the pianist; there is no statement that the pianist became angry, as option 4 claims.
I very much hope people will use this valuable program as an opportunity to teach children good manners.
Means to teach someone something; 子どもに identifies the learners and マナーを the content.
Means as, here as a setting for teaching manners.
Expresses a wish for someone else to do something.
Q2: Directly states the purpose of teaching children manners, matching option 1, a place to learn manners.
Children should be clearly told to stay quiet during the performance.
Tells someone to do something; に after よう is omitted here.
Indicates the time during which an activity is taking place.
If children can no longer stay quiet, they must be taken out of the hall immediately.
Expresses a change to no longer doing or being able to do something.
Means when; combined here with もしも to introduce a hypothetical situation.
A dictionary-form verb followed by sentence-final こと states a rule or instruction: leave immediately.
Children will understand as they gain experience.
Expresses a condition: if they gain experience, they will understand.
In fact, many children did stay quiet that day.
how many people; many with も
Describes an ongoing past action or state, here staying quiet.
何人も with an affirmative predicate means many people.
Highlights a fact that explains or supports the preceding point.
I would also like the organizers to make considerate arrangements, such as providing parents and children with seats near the aisle for easy access.
Attaches to a noun to identify intended users: 親子用 means for parents and children.
Verb stem plus やすい means easy to do; 出入りしやすい means easy to enter and leave.
Introduces an example of the consideration requested from the organizers.
Means also, extending the request to the organizers.
A humble, polite way to express a wish for someone to do something for the speaker.
Q3: Requests seats for parents and children, specifically near the aisle for easy access; option 4 is correct.
I hope this wonderful program will continue for a long time in a way that satisfies everyone.
Means everyone, affirming something about all people.
Means in a way that; the preceding clause modifies 形.
Expresses a hope that something will happen; に after よう is omitted.
(Note 1) 幾度となく: over and over again.
Means many times in an affirmative expression; repetition emphasizes recurrence.
(Note 2) 合間: a short interval before the next activity takes place.
Passive form: 行なう → 行なわれる, meaning to be carried out.
Modifies a noun with a time endpoint: the interval until the next activity takes place.
Introduces a concert admitting children from age zero; the writer praises the performance but expresses disappointment with some attendees' manners.
Frequent movement in and out and repeated noise from children led a listener to intervene; this explains the poor manners.
The writer wants children to learn manners through experience: they should be told to stay quiet and taken outside if they cannot. Many children that day managed to stay quiet.
Request to organizers and long-term hope
Requests seats near the aisle for parents and children and hopes the program will continue in a way that satisfies everyone.
Defines 幾度となく as repeatedly and 合間 as a short interval before the next activity.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t25-p1.vietnamese:
The other day, a piano concert admitting children from age zero was held at a hall in the ward. The performance was wonderful, but I was disappointed by some people's poor manners.

Even during the performance, people kept going in and out of the hall, and children's voices rang out again and again. It was so bad that a man seated toward the front turned around between pieces twice to say, “Please be quiet.” I really felt sorry for the pianist.

I very much hope people will use this valuable program as an opportunity to teach children good manners. Children should be clearly told to stay quiet during the performance. If they can no longer stay quiet, they must be taken out of the hall immediately. Children will understand as they gain experience. In fact, many children did stay quiet that day. I would also like the organizers to make considerate arrangements, such as providing parents and children with seats near the aisle for easy access. I hope this wonderful program will continue for a long time in a way that satisfies everyone.

(Note 1) 幾度となく: over and over again.

(Note 2) 合間: a short interval before the next activity takes place.
The new school term has begun, and children make their way happily to school along the school route in front of our house.
The continuative form of 始まる links the beginning of the term to the scene of children going to school.
を marks the route traversed: 通学路を means along the school route.
An adjective stem plus そうに describes how someone appears while acting; 楽しそうに means looking happy.
Expresses movement away from the narrator's viewpoint.
The girls' chatter is as ceaseless as the chirping of little birds.
A noun plus のように expresses comparison: like birdsong. Here ように does not express purpose.
Since my husband and I both like children, we go outside and call out, “Have a good day!”
have a good day (said to someone leaving)
Indicates that both share the same characteristic: both the husband and narrator like children.
が marks the person or thing someone likes.
Gives a reason; 好き is a な-adjective, so it takes だから.
Links successive actions: going outside and then greeting the children.
と marks the words called out to someone.
Direct evidence for Question 3, option 1: the couple go outside and greet the passing children.
Three years ago, while serving on the neighborhood association's committee, I agreed to make our home a “Children's 110” safety house.
designated safety house where children can seek help
Describes an activity or state continuing at a past time.
Specifies when the action occurred: while serving on the neighborhood committee.
The children rarely stop by on their way to or from school, but having no reason to seek help is evidence that the neighborhood is safe, so it is something to be glad about.
on the way to or from school
A dictionary-form verb plus こと nominalizes an event; めったに～ない means rarely. This is not the concessive repetition pattern VことはVが.
Connects contrasting ideas: the children rarely visit, but that is welcome.
のは presents an event as the topic; だから gives the reason for the positive evaluation.
A formal written equivalent of だ or です, used in 安全である and ことである.
Main evidence for Question 1, option 2: having no need for help signals safety, indicating that the house serves to support and protect children.
Children rarely stop by; visits alone do not define the house's main purpose in Question 1.
Occasionally, a girl comes almost rushing in and says, “May I use your toilet, please?”
A polite request; トイレを貸してください asks permission to use the toilet.
Here it describes manner: entering as if rushing in. It is not ようにしている expressing a deliberate habit.
Expresses movement toward the narrator's location.
An example of everyday help; it shows that option 4 in Question 1 describes a specific service rather than the house's overall purpose.
In summer, boys also stop by and ask, “May I have some water, please?”
に marks time, while は presents summer as the topic.
A noun plus をください is used to ask for something.
Means also: boys visit too, in addition to the girls mentioned earlier.
Another example of helping children; together with the previous sentence, it shows that water and toilet access are specific activities in Question 1.
は sets autumn as the topic; が marks dusk as what comes early.
The dusk setting supports Question 2: the following event occurs as children head home, rather than on their morning trip to school.

There was also an occasion when a child said, “It's getting dark and I'm scared. Could you take me home?” My husband accompanied the child by bicycle, and was relieved to meet a family member who had come to pick the child up along the way.
uncle (a child's friendly address to an older man)
Replace an い-adjective's final い with くなる to express change: 暗くなる means to get dark.
Gives the reason for the request: it is dark and the child is scared.
Marks the destination or endpoint: 家まで means all the way home.
A sentence-final て-form makes an informal request; 送って asks someone to take the speaker home.
と quotes the child's words, and ので explains why the husband accompanies the child.
で marks the means of transport: 自転車で means by bicycle.
Here it narrates a result on a particular occasion: when he accompanied the child, he met a family member.
A verb stem plus に来る expresses the purpose of coming: 迎えに来る means to come to pick someone up.
来られた is the honorific form of 来た here, showing respect for the family member who came.
会え is the continuative form of the potential verb 会える, meaning was able to meet; it is not an imperative here.
Expresses that something has also happened on an occasion. The original ends with ことも, leaving ある or あった understood.
Evidence for Question 2, option 3: the child needs to get home after dark, so 途中 refers to the journey home from school. It also illustrates the protective role in Question 1.
途中 is the route on which the husband is accompanying the child home and meets the arriving family member, not a walk or a trip to the neighborhood association.
The embankment along the school route also serves as a walking path for adults.
に marks a role, も adds also, and ている describes the current state: the place also serves as a walking path.
The passage opens with cheerful children heading to school. The couple like children and go outside to greet them, directly supporting Question 3, option 1.
The role of the children's safety house
The narrator took on the role of providing a safety house. Children's lack of need for help is seen as evidence of neighborhood safety, clarifying its protective purpose in Question 1, option 2.
Children sometimes ask to use the toilet or have water. These are specific examples of assistance rather than the house's full purpose, helping distinguish option 4 in Question 1.
Accompanying a child home after dark

With autumn's early dusk, the husband once accompanied a child home and met a family member coming to pick the child up. This identifies 途中 as the journey home from school in Question 2, option 3, and illustrates the protective role. The last sentence adds that adults also walk along the embankment.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t26-p1.vietnamese:
The new school term has begun, and children make their way happily to school along the school route in front of our house. The girls' chatter is as ceaseless as the chirping of little birds. Since my husband and I both like children, we go outside and call out, “Have a good day!”

Three years ago, while serving on the neighborhood association's committee, I agreed to make our home a “Children's 110” safety house. The children rarely stop by on their way to or from school, but having no reason to seek help is evidence that the neighborhood is safe, so it is something to be glad about.

Occasionally, a girl comes almost rushing in and says, “May I use your toilet, please?” In summer, boys also stop by and ask, “May I have some water, please?”

In autumn, dusk comes early. There was also an occasion when a child said, “It's getting dark and I'm scared. Could you take me home?” My husband accompanied the child by bicycle, and was relieved to meet a family member who had come to pick the child up along the way. The embankment along the school route also serves as a walking path for adults.
My English teacher when I was in seventh grade was in charge of social studies but also taught English, and I couldn't feel any enthusiasm from them at all.
Although / despite... (expresses contrast, dissatisfaction, or surprise contrary to expectation).
Not at all / completely not... (used with a negative verb for complete negation).
Potential or spontaneous form of the verb 感じる (can feel / be felt).
Because he lacked confidence in his pronunciation, his voice in class was soft, and there was no pronunciation guidance at all.
Because / since... (expresses an objective reason or cause).
Continuative form of an i-adjective (小さい → 小さく) used to connect descriptive clauses.
Direct evidence for the '発音指導はしなかった' clause in correct option 4 of Q1 (the teacher gave no pronunciation instruction).
Shows the teacher lacked confidence in pronunciation, directly confirming option 2 in Q3 and disproving option 1 in Q1 (he spoke quietly due to low confidence, not loudly).
Homework was mostly nothing but writing each vocabulary word 100 times.
Such as / like... (used to give specific examples representing a category).
Nothing but / only... (emphasizes exclusivity or repetition, often with a nuance of dissatisfaction).
Demonstrates that the teacher did teach vocabulary (by assigning students to write words 100 times each), confirming '単語は教えた' in correct option 4 of Q1.
In the second year, when our teacher changed to an English specialist, I was shocked by the difference in the lesson content.
Change to / be replaced by... (indicates a transition or change of person/state).
Be surprised / astonished at... (particle に marks the cause of the emotional reaction).
We couldn't even read phonetic symbols and didn't understand grammar, so for a while, we couldn't keep up with the classes.
Even... (presents an extreme or minimal example to emphasize severity).
Formal/written negative continuative form equivalent to ないで / なくて (without doing... / not doing...).
To keep up with... (here in negative potential past: could not keep up with).

Ever since then, an aversion to English took root; although I got through entrance exams by rote memorization, I still carry a feeling of inferiority when it comes to communication skills like listening and speaking.
To end up doing... (expresses an unintended action with regrettable consequences).
About / concerning... (introduces a topic or subject matter under consideration).
Currently, how many elementary school teachers are there who can teach English with confidence?
I wonder how many there are
With confidence (holding confidence while performing an action).
I wonder if... / Could it be that...? (expresses self-questioning, concern, or contemplation).
Children probably won't grow even if they are taught by a teacher who lacks confidence.
Even if... (expresses a concessive conditional: even if the condition is met, the desired outcome does not occur).
Probably / likely (expresses the speaker's conjecture or assessment).
Explicitly characterizes unconfident teachers as unable to foster student progress, providing the direct rationale for correct option 2 in Q3 (taught by an unconfident teacher).
If teacher quality cannot be ensured, I wish they would not make it compulsory.
wish / want them not to make
If... / in case... (sets a contextual condition for a request or judgment).
I wish you/they would not do... (expresses a desire for someone not to perform an action).
Direct evidence stating the condition/reason why the author opposes making English compulsory in elementary schools: teacher quality cannot be guaranteed (corresponding to option 1 of Q2).
Five years from now, when my own child enters elementary school, I wonder what the situation will be like.
I wonder what will have become of it
Around the time when... (indicates an approximate time or period).
I wonder how it is / will be turning out (combination of progressive form and reflective question).
Whatever happens, I sincerely hope they will not subject them to the exact kind of education we experienced.
Earnestly wish someone to do / not do something (どうか at the beginning intensifies the plea).
At least please don't do that / only that I wish to avoid (emphasizes avoiding a specific worst-case outcome).
(Note) Social studies: one of the subject courses, teaching topics such as human geography and history.
Being one of... (used to define or classify an item within a broader category).
Teach such things as... (lists representative examples non-exhaustively).
The author recounts learning English from an unenthusiastic social studies teacher lacking pronunciation confidence, contrasted with the switch to a specialist in eighth grade.
Students suffered severe knowledge gaps in pronunciation and grammar, resulting in long-term insecurity regarding English communication skills.
Views on elementary English and parental concerns
Reflecting on teachers lacking confidence, the author opposes making elementary English compulsory without quality standards and hopes their child will not repeat past educational mistakes.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t27-p1.vietnamese:
My English teacher when I was in seventh grade was originally in charge of social studies but also taught English, and I could not feel any enthusiasm from him at all.

Because he lacked confidence in his pronunciation, his voice during class was quiet, and he provided no pronunciation instruction whatsoever. Homework was also nothing but things like copying each vocabulary word 100 times. In our second year, our teacher changed to an English specialist, and I was astonished by the sheer difference in lesson content.

We could not even read phonetic symbols and did not understand grammar, so for a while, we were unable to keep up with the class. Ever since then, an aversion to English took root in me; while I managed to get through entrance examinations through rote memorization, I still carry an inferiority complex to this day when it comes to communication skills such as listening and speaking.

At present, I wonder just how many elementary school teachers can actually teach English with confidence. Children will likely not grow even if taught by a teacher who lacks confidence. If teacher quality cannot be guaranteed, please do not make it a compulsory subject. Five years from now, when my own child enters elementary school, what will things look like? By all means, I sincerely hope they will never subject children to the kind of education we experienced.

(Note) Social studies: A subject course within the school curriculum that teaches subjects such as human geography and history.
When it comes to peeling fruit, monkeys apparently rival humans.
Nominalizes a verb: 剥くこと means the act of peeling.
When it comes to…; highlights a field in which someone excels.
Apparently…; expresses a judgment based on information or evidence.
The opening states the overall observation about monkeys' ability to peel fruit, supporting option 2 for Question 2.
If a mischievous spectator happens to toss the monkeys a rakkyo bulb, quite a commotion ensues.
Presents an action as an example, here tossing a rakkyo bulb to the monkeys.
If/when…; introduces the result of the preceding situation.
In 大変なことになる, means that things turn troublesome; it does not express a decision here.
First, a sharp-eyed young monkey spots it before the others, walks slowly over, picks it up very gently with its fingertips, and looks at it in puzzlement.
In 目の早い, の replaces が within a noun-modifying phrase: quick-eyed.
Indicates movement away from a reference point; here, walking over to the bulb.
With an apparently… look; describes the outward manner of an action.
Verb stems and te-forms link successive actions: spotting, approaching, picking up, and looking.
This is the behavior asked about in Question 1; its cause is explained in the next sentence.
Apparently having never seen anything like it before, it examines the bulb vertically and horizontally; finally seeming reassured, it begins peeling it slowly and carefully.
Have never…; expresses a lack of prior experience.
Not even once; emphasizes complete absence of an experience.
The connective form of らしい: apparently…; infers unfamiliarity from the monkey's behavior.
Seems… and…; links an inferred state of reassurance to the next action.
Attaches to a verb's masu-stem to mean begin doing: 剥き＋始める.
Having never seen it before, the monkey does not know what it has been given: direct support for option 2 in Question 1.
The peeling illustrates the opening observation and supports option 2 in Question 2; it also weighs against the claim in Question 1 that the monkey does not know how to peel it.
Repeating the same counted unit conveys succession; the peeling action is omitted but understood from the previous sentence.
Because the flesh still fails to appear, it seems to grow impatient and now works its fingers busily.
Still does not…; an expected result is slow or difficult to occur.
In 出てくる, describes something emerging into view.
Because…; gives the cause of the impatience.
Apparently…; the narrator infers the monkey's feelings from its actions.
The monkey becomes frustrated because the expected flesh never appears; together with the closing appeal, this supports the sympathetic interpretation in option 4 of Question 3.
The negative form of ～てくる; the subject 実 is omitted because it was stated in the previous sentence.
Just as it pauses in disappointment and lets its guard down, another monkey suddenly appears, snatches the now smaller rakkyo bulb, and promptly runs off.
Just as someone is…; a new event intrudes into an ongoing situation.
An i-adjective takes ～く＋なる to express change: 小さくなった means became smaller.
A clause modifies a noun: 小さくなった describes ラッキョウ.
Attaches to a verb stem; 逃げ出す means to start running away or make an escape.
Explicitly describes the monkey's disappointment; along with its fruitless peeling and the closing appeal, this supports option 4 in Question 3.
Startled, the first monkey hurriedly gives chase.
びっくりした modifies 前の猿: the earlier monkey, now startled.
慌てて describes the flustered manner in which the monkey gives chase.
In an instant, the other young monkeys all give chase too, looking ready to pounce.
A verb stem plus そうに describes seeming about to act; here, looking ready to pounce, without stating that they actually do.
Also…; the other monkeys join the first monkey in giving chase.
The parent monkeys glance at the commotion as they move leisurely over the rocks.
While…; the same subject moves and watches at the same time.
を marks the route or area traversed: 岩場の上を means over the rocky area.
Describes an action in progress within the observed scene.
I earnestly ask all visitors to heed this request.
Addresses a request to the person or group marked by に.
Intensifies an earnest request or reminder; the specific request follows in the next sentence.
The earnest appeal introduces the request not to give monkeys things they do not eat, supporting the sympathetic attitude in Question 3.
Please do not give the monkeys things they do not eat.
猿が食べない modifies もの: things monkeys do not eat.
Please do not…; asks the listener to refrain from an action.
Together with the monkey's frustration and disappointment, the final request shows that the author considers giving it rakkyo unkind: option 4 in Question 3.
States the central observation: monkeys rival humans at peeling fruit. This is the overall point for Question 2.
Inspecting and peeling an unfamiliar object
A spectator tosses a rakkyo bulb to the monkeys. A young monkey looks puzzled because it has never seen one before, then cautiously starts peeling.
Peeling layer after layer without finding the expected flesh makes the monkey impatient and disappointed. When it pauses, another monkey steals the bulb.
Young monkeys chase; parents remain calm
The young monkeys all give chase, while the parent monkeys merely glance over as they move leisurely across the rocks.
The author earnestly asks visitors not to give monkeys things they do not eat. In light of the preceding events, the ending supports the view that giving them rakkyo is unkind.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t28-p1.vietnamese:
When it comes to peeling fruit, monkeys apparently rival humans.

If a mischievous spectator happens to toss the monkeys a rakkyo bulb, quite a commotion ensues. First, a sharp-eyed young monkey spots it before the others, walks slowly over, picks it up very gently with its fingertips, and looks at it in puzzlement. Apparently having never seen anything like it before, it examines the bulb vertically and horizontally; finally seeming reassured, it begins peeling it slowly and carefully. One layer, then another. Because the flesh still fails to appear, it seems to grow impatient and now works its fingers busily. Still, no flesh appears. Just as it pauses in disappointment and lets its guard down, another monkey suddenly appears, snatches the now smaller rakkyo bulb, and promptly runs off. Startled, the first monkey hurriedly gives chase. In an instant, the other young monkeys all give chase too, looking ready to pounce. The parent monkeys glance at the commotion as they move leisurely over the rocks.

I earnestly ask all visitors to heed this request. Please do not give the monkeys things they do not eat.
When I was in elementary school, an elderly woman I did not know asked me for directions.
Indicates the time period when something happened.
Passive form: to have something done by someone.
However, because my mother had told me, “You must not talk to strangers,” all I could manage to say was, “I don't know.”
Marks the topic or object being referred to.
Colloquial form of ～てはだめ, meaning must not do something.
Describes something one had been told or instructed.
Indicates that this was all one could manage.
Because many abduction incidents have been occurring, even though I understand that my mother's advice was meant to protect me, I cannot forget the elderly woman's lonely-looking face.
Indicates a cause or purpose; here it indicates a cause.
Negative potential form, meaning cannot do something.
The girl still remembers the elderly woman's lonely face; seeing her look sad also caused the child pain.
My younger brother, who was about the same age as I was then, learned that “when criminals are greeted first by children, their murderous intent weakens,” so he began a greeting campaign on his own.
Expresses an approximate degree or amount.
Emphasizes the side that takes the initiative.
Indicates the condition of being done something.
Connects actions in sequence or with a cause-and-result relationship.
Apparently, when he greets adults he passes on his way to or from school, he always receives a reply.
Indicates the time when an action takes place.
Indicates a result that regularly occurs under that condition.
Conveys information heard from someone else.
Recently, he looked happy as he said that he also received words such as “See you later” and “It's cold today, isn't it?”
Gives representative examples, meaning such as…

I think many adults feel lonely when children run away even after they speak to them, but the children who run away also suffer. I hope we can live in a society where people can speak to one another without fear.
even if one speaks to someone
be able to speak to one another
Expresses a personal thought or opinion softly.
Potential form, meaning be able to do something.
Expresses a wish for a state to become a certain way.
The writer hopes for a safe society where people can greet one another without fearing criminals.
The girl was told not to talk to strangers, so she could not help the elderly woman and remained troubled by her lonely face.
The younger brother learns that children greeting first may reduce criminals' harmful intent, so he greets adults and receives friendly replies.
A wish for a safe society
Adults feel sad when children avoid them, while children also suffer when they have to run away; therefore, the writer hopes people can greet one another safely.
default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t29-p1.vietnamese:
When I was in elementary school, an elderly woman I did not know asked me for directions. However, because my mother had told me, “You must not talk to strangers,” all I could manage to say was, “I don't know.”

Because many abduction incidents have been occurring, even though I understand that my mother's advice was meant to protect me, I cannot forget the elderly woman's lonely-looking face.

My younger brother, who was about the same age as I was then, learned that “when criminals are greeted first by children, their murderous intent weakens,” so he began a greeting campaign on his own.

Apparently, when he greets adults he passes on his way to or from school, he always receives a reply. Recently, he looked happy as he said that he also received words such as “See you later” and “It's cold today, isn't it?”

I think many adults feel lonely when children run away even after they speak to them, but the children who run away also suffer. I hope we can live in a society where people can speak to one another without fear.
Country A and Country B have been fighting a fierce war for many years now.
Emphasizes a large quantity or long duration; 何年も means for many years.
Expresses an ongoing action; the war has continued and is still in progress.
Every day, hundreds of thousands of people are dying.
も emphasizes the very large number: as many as hundreds of thousands of people.
With 毎日, describes a situation that keeps recurring every day.
Questions 2 and 3: the daily loss of life supports the antiwar message and contrasts with the death-free day at the end.
The polite past form of です, identifying what that day was.
A few soldiers came out from Country A's army, holding a white flag and a bottle of wine.
Marks the point of departure: from Country A's army.
Describes an accompanying state: coming out while holding or carrying something.
Expresses movement toward the scene's viewpoint; 出てくる means to come out or emerge.
Question 1: the white flag, wine, and following invitation indicate a peaceful approach. In this context, option 2, “We are not carrying weapons,” fits rather than an admission of defeat.
“Hey, folks from Country B, why don't we enjoy Christmas together?”
a polite or friendly form of address
A negative-form question used as a casual invitation: why don't we…?
Question 1: the invitation confirms the friendly purpose of the white flag, rather than a declaration of victory or defeat.
Then soldiers from Country B's army also came out, carrying wine and grilled meat.
Combines a point of departure with “also”: soldiers come out from B's side too.
Lists examples without implying that the list is exhaustive.
A nonpast form appears within a past narrative to make the scene vivid; it does not indicate a future event.
The soldiers of both countries sat on the ground, drinking, eating, and singing.
Both… and…; emphasizes participation by soldiers from both sides.
The stem before ます links actions in written language; 座り connects sitting down with the following activities.
Lists representative activities without necessarily specifying their chronological order.
Question 3: soldiers on both sides choose peaceful interaction, showing that people can stop fighting.
The number of people taking part kept growing rapidly.
Expresses a change continuing from the narrative moment: the number keeps increasing.
A soldier from Country A said:
“Instead of fighting some war, we should play a soccer match and count whichever side wins as the winner.”
if one does; if one counts as
Follows a noun to express dismissal or rejection; here it conveys opposition to war.
Do the second action without doing the first: play sports instead of fighting.
Identifies the side that performed an action: 勝ったほう is the side that won. This is not the advice pattern ～たほうがいい.
Decide on or treat something as a particular outcome; here the match determines who wins.
Offers a solution or suggestion: all we need to do is…
The casual form of のだ, adding explanatory emphasis to the speaker's view.
Question 2: なんか dismisses war, supporting option 4, “Enough of war.” In that option, たくさんだ means “have had enough.”
Question 3: the soldier proposes replacing fighting with a match, supporting the idea that people can end war.
A soldier from Country B also spoke up:
Means “also”: a soldier from B speaks after the soldier from A.
Introduces a condition or topic: if it is basketball; when it comes to basketball.
A sentence-final particle adding force and confidence in casual speech.
That day, soccer and basketball matches were held between Country A and Country B.
Indicates an event involving the specified parties: between Countries A and B.
The passive form; 行なわれました means were conducted or held.
Question 3: the proposed matches actually take place; the soldiers choose peaceful activities instead of fighting that day.
Country A won at soccer, while Country B won at basketball.
Sets a domain and contrasts outcomes: A wins in soccer, while B wins in basketball.
Of course, not a single person died that day.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
Japanese normally uses three types of characters: kanji, hiragana, and katakana.

Kanji are characters that originated in China to represent the Chinese language. It is said that the original form of kanji already existed about three thousand years ago. Kanji in its present form reached Japan about sixteen hundred years ago. At that time, Japan still had nothing called a writing system. At first, the Japanese arranged only kanji to represent the Japanese language. Regardless of the original meanings of the kanji, they used kanji readings to write down the sounds of Japanese. However, this method was inconvenient because both memorizing and writing it took a great deal of time. Therefore, based on kanji, the Japanese invented characters that represented only sounds: katakana and hiragana.

Katakana was generally created by taking part of a kanji. For example, “カ” was made from “加,” and “リ” was made from “利.” Hiragana was created by cursively transforming entire kanji. For example, “せ” was formed by transforming “世,” and “れ” by transforming “礼.” Kana began to be used widely from the Heian period. Thanks to the invention of kana, Japanese culture developed greatly.

Roman letters originated from Egyptian writing. Roman letters reached Japan in the sixteenth century, but Japanese began to be written in Roman letters only from the Meiji period.

(Note 1) Heian period: a Japanese era lasting about 400 years from 794.

(Note 2) Meiji period: a Japanese era from 1868 to 1912.

If we think about it, greetings such as “good morning” and “hello” may also seem like meaningless words. It is hard to understand saying “good morning” even when it is nearly noon, simply because it is still before noon. Also, saying “hello” does not actually mean asking “What happened today?”, so there apparently are people who consider such expressions completely meaningless.

However, we probably should not think of greetings in that way. When we greet one another with expressions such as “good morning” or “hello,” with cheerful faces and voices, we can convey feelings of friendliness; that is where the meaning of greetings lies.

In fact, this applies not only to greetings: language is fundamentally a means of trying to convey our thoughts to another person. When we use language, we communicate our thoughts and feelings to others. Alternatively, through language, we learn about their thoughts and feelings. We could also say that social life is sustained by language.

To get along smoothly in society each day, we must pay attention to how we use words. This is because words can sometimes make people happy and sometimes make them sad. We should avoid words and ways of speaking that upset others or cause them to misunderstand us, and use words with one another that brighten both their spirits and our own—in other words, words that make social life brighter.

default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
In Japan, people take off their shoes when entering a house. This is a longstanding custom aimed at keeping dirt out of the home, as Japan's highly humid climate makes footwear easily soiled. Nowadays, roads are paved and people no longer need to worry about dirt as much as in the past, yet this custom continues to this day.

In student dormitories, people take off their shoes at the entrance in most cases, but wear indoor footwear (such as slippers) in shared spaces like dining halls and corridors. Each resident prepares these separately from their outdoor shoes. In addition, removed shoes are stored either in individual shoe lockers or inside one's own room.

When entering a Japanese-style room (a traditional room with tatami mats), one must without fail remove all footwear. Recently, however, even in Japanese residences, homes consisting purely of Japanese-style rooms are rare, and styles incorporating Western-style rooms have become common. In the kitchen and living room, wearing indoor footwear is standard practice.

Housing issues in urban areas surrounding Tokyo are a serious matter even for Japanese citizens. In particular, in apartment complexes where cramped rooms and expensive rents are taken for granted, soundproofing is usually not equipped, so it is normal for residents to mutually tolerate a certain level of daily living noise.

Student dormitories face the same reality: while minor sounds cannot be helped, loud noise is a completely different matter. First and foremost, individuals must be mindful of their own actions; furthermore, if noise persists or conflicts arise, it is advisable to consult the landlord, dorm director, or manager.

(Note) Living noise: Various sounds generated in the course of daily living.

We see objects with our eyes and can know their shape, size, and color. In addition, through the function of both left and right eyes, we are able to distinguish whether an object is far or near. Moreover, the eyes are spaced apart to the left and right, allowing us to see a wide range. When we use our hands, we can grasp or move objects. default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t37-p1.vietnamese:
Today, let us talk about Japanese cuisine in general, including fish, which the Japanese people love so dearly. When fish is mentioned, the first thing that comes to mind is sashimi. For those who say that raw food does not suit their taste at all, I recommend cooked dishes. Even though we simply refer to it as 'heating,' there is truly a wide variety, starting from 'simmering' to 'steaming,' 'boiling,' 'grilling,' 'stir-frying,' and 'searing.' Regarding the way heat is applied, I think it can be broadly divided into two categories: boiling water to 'simmer or boil' (such as potatoes and eggs), utilizing that steam to 'steam' (such as manju buns), and using oil instead of water to 'coat in batter and deep-fry' (such as tempura and croquettes).

Vegetables that children are generally reluctant to eat are often eaten quite well when stir-fried in a frying pan with oil. This can be called an indirect method. In contrast to this, the direct method involves placing chicken, fish, or other ingredients on a wire mesh and heating them directly over charcoal embers. This is 'grilling.' Even with the same fish, when dried, it becomes 'searing.' When grilling, careful ingenuity is required. You must neither hold it too far from the flame nor bring it too close. If you ask how to achieve a distance that is neither too far nor too close, that subtle gap is the key. In the case of meat and similar items, judging from the degree of doneness, whether it is better well-done or lightly cooked is purely a matter of personal preference.

Lastly, regarding 'three-minute boiling water' instant noodles, while they are not so bad as to be called a disgrace to Japanese cuisine, I am currently wondering whether such a thing can even be called cooking.

(Note) Instant noodles: Noodles that can be eaten immediately after adding hot water. For example, instant ramen is one of them.

This year too, on the morning of New Year's Day (Gantan)—that is, the morning of January 1st—there were many 'New Year cards' in our mailbox. In normal years, leisurely looking through them one by one while wondering who sent cards this year or whether someone you haven't seen in a while is doing well is one of the joys of the New Year season. However, this year things were a bit different. The moment I saw the pile of New Year cards, I suddenly felt rushed: 'Oh no, this is trouble! I have to write replies quickly and go drop them in the mailbox before the day ends.'

I think New Year cards are a wonderful custom that allows you to express your gratitude to people who helped you during the past year, and to let each other know once a year that you are staying healthy—connecting with old friends you rarely have the chance to meet or relatives living far away. However, writing and mailing hundreds of cards during December, the busiest time of the year, so that they arrive on New Year's Day of the coming year is truly an arduous chore. So this time, I decided not to write them in December, but rather to write replies only to those people from whom I received cards once New Year arrived. When I made that decision, I even thought to myself that it was a fairly clever method. But when New Year actually arrived and I saw the large pile of cards, I ultimately found myself thinking: 'I should have sent the cards out in December after all.'

(Note) 郵便受け (mailbox): A box or receptacle into which postal items such as letters are placed.

I picked up a car key. Since it was lying dropped at the entrance of the parking lot of the apartment building next to my home, it probably belonged to someone living there. They might be in trouble, and I wanted to return it to them quickly. While pondering over this, I remembered the time back in elementary school when I had lost my house key.

Realizing that I had dropped it, I imagined a burglar picking up that key. The burglar would go around the neighborhood house by house in the middle of the night, searching for the house matching the key. Then, the burglar would arrive at my house. Inserting the key into the keyhole to open the front door, the burglar would break right into the house. I was completely terrified, so I pleaded with my parents and finally had our house lock replaced.

Now, as for this car key, should I go to the parking lot in the middle of the night and try inserting it into each car door? default.p.115dokkai_choubun_n3-t47-p1.vietnamese:
Dear Sir,

Dear Professor Tanaka. It has been a long time. Have you been well? I am writing today because there is something I would like to consult you about.

I started working at a small company in Tokyo two years ago, but recently I have been growing tired of the job. Day after day, I am made to do nothing but tedious paperwork sorting, and I cannot do the work I want to do. On top of that, I do not find the people I work with particularly appealing either. My colleague Yamada is always thinking about flattering the boss (Note 1), and when the boss is absent, he does nothing but doze off. My current boss also likes finding fault with my work, which sometimes makes me angry. My previous boss, though, was trustworthy and very good.

However, the pay at this company is not bad. Of course, I do not intend to stay at this company for long, but I plan to work here for another six months and save up the tuition fees to study at a business school in the United States in the future.

I must submit my application (Note 2) to the business school by the summer. Therefore, I am sorry to trouble you, but could you please write me a letter of recommendation by July? I would greatly appreciate your help.

Yours sincerely,

June 12, 2004

Kimura Hiroshi

To Professor Tanaka

Dear Mr. Blanc,

Cold days are still continuing; how have you been doing, Mr. Blanc?

I arrived in New York on December 10th, and light snow was falling. Since my flight arrived late at night, I did not go anywhere that day and went straight to my hotel in Manhattan, falling fast asleep.

The next day, I woke up around noon. The snow outside had stopped, and from the window I could see tall buildings, yellow cabs, and people walking busily. My room received plenty of sunlight and had high ceilings. The window set into the white wall was also large, making the room very pleasant.

In the evening, I went into town to do some shopping. The Christmas decorations were truly beautiful, and I visited many shops. New York truly has items from all kinds of countries. I decided to buy a matching pair of watches as a gift for my parents.

On the way back, four or five people were gathered around a narrow entrance of a building. Among them, a woman had fallen down, and a police officer was in the middle of asking her what had happened. The woman had a handbag and large luggage, but the handbag was open and there was nothing left inside. I felt a little frightened. However, the people walking behind me did not even glance at the woman; they were merely hurrying along the cold night street.

Since I have only just arrived in the United States, I think there are still many things I do not understand. Even so, by seeing and hearing many things, I hope to continue experiencing American society firsthand. It will get even colder from here on, so please take good care of yourself.

December 15th

Dear Kazuko,

How are you? Tomorrow will mark exactly six months since I came to graduate school in Beijing. It gets a little colder every day, and it snowed yesterday. This year, there were few truly hot summer days, and a cool summer continued throughout.

During summer vacation, I also took part in volunteer activities in my hometown, so I had hardly any days that felt like a real vacation. I am currently studying in an advanced Chinese class, but I am still slow at both writing and reading, so doing my homework takes a long time. In particular, the Chinese classical literature class is difficult. It would be good if I could read books without using a dictionary, but I still cannot do that. During tests, dictionaries are not allowed, so I sometimes have trouble.

Oh right, I had not written about my roommate yet. My roommate is from America, and her name is Marie. Marie can speak French and German, and she can also read a little Japanese. Besides that, she is very good at cooking. Last Sunday, there was a garden party at the home of a Chinese friend who lives in the suburbs, and I went there. Since it had been decided that each person would make one specialty dish, I was in a difficult situation. Having no other choice, I asked Chen to make it for me. I got to meet many different people, and it was a very enjoyable party.

Please come visit me while I am in Beijing. I would like to show you the beautiful university campus. The upcoming New Year’s holiday would be fine too. Please let me know when it is convenient for you.

Finally, please give my regards to everyone in your household.

November 10

Kumi
